Consequently, $v_{0}=h_{s-3}(w_{1})\in h_{s-3}(Y_{s-4})\subset X_{s-3},$ which contradicts the previous claim.

Iterating this procedure, we successively construct $v_{0},\cdots,v_{s}$ and $w_{0},\cdots,w_{s}$ satisfying the required conditions.

(3) By (2), there exist vertices $v_{0},v_{1},\dots,v_{s}=v\in X_{v}$ and $w_{0}=w,\dots,w_{s}\in Y_{v}$ such that for all $0\leq i\leq s$ , $h_{s}(w_{i})=v_{i}$ and $h_{s-1}(w_{i+1})=v_{i}.$ Then the corresponding edges $e_{w_{i}}=[w_{i},w_{i}^{\prime}]$ and $e_{v_{i}}=[v_{i},v_{i}^{\prime}]$ satisfy $h_{s}(e_{w_{i}})=e_{v_{i}}$ and $h_{s-1}(e_{w_{i+1}})=e_{v_{i}}.$ In particular, $h_{s}(w_{i}^{\prime})=v_{i}^{\prime}$ and $h_{s-1}(w_{i+1}^{\prime})=v_{i}^{\prime}.$ Applying (2) once again, we conclude that $w^{\prime}\in Y_{v^{\prime}}.$

(4) Let $X_{v}=\{v_{i}\}_{1\leq i\leq l},$ and $Y_{v}=\{w_{j}\}_{1\leq j\leq l^{\prime}}.$ By Proposition 4.7(2), there exists $m\in\mathbb{N}$ large enough such that $\mu_{f}(f^{m}(v_{i}))=\mu_{f}(f^{m+1}(w_{j}))=1$ for all $1\leq i\leq l$ and $1\leq j\leq l^{\prime}$ . Note that $\mu_{f}=\mu_{g}$ . By Proposition 4.7(3), we may define

$$ \displaystyle d_{i} \displaystyle\coloneqq\deg_{v_{i}}f^{m}=\deg_{v_{i}}g^{m}=d^{m}\mu_{f}(v_{i}) \displaystyle\delta_{j} \displaystyle\coloneqq\deg_{w_{j}}f^{m+1}=\deg_{w_{j}}g^{m+1}=d^{m+1}\mu_{f}(w_{j}) $$

For each $j$ , there exist indices $i_{j}$ and $k_{j}$ such that $f$ (resp. $g$ ) maps $D_{w_{j}}$ onto $D_{v_{i_{j}}}$ (resp. $D_{v_{k_{j}}}$ ). We then have $\deg_{w_{j}}f=\frac{\delta_{j}}{d_{i_{j}}},$ and $\deg_{w_{j}}g=\frac{\delta_{j}}{d_{k_{j}}}.$

Now choose a finite set $A\subset\bigcup_{i=1}^{l}(D_{v_{i}}\cap k)$ such that $\#(A\cap D_{v_{i}})=d_{i}$ for each $1\leq i\leq l$ . Then, for every $w_{j}\in Y_{v}$ , the number of preimages of $A$ under $f$ in $D_{w_{j}}$ is $d_{i_{j}}\cdot\frac{\delta_{j}}{d_{i_{j}}}=\delta_{j},$ and similarly the number of preimages under $g$ in $D_{w_{j}}$ is $d_{k_{j}}\cdot\frac{\delta_{j}}{d_{k_{j}}}=\delta_{j}.$ ∎

### 5.2. Rigidity of Julia sets for polynomials of the same degree

Recall that for the Julia set $\mathcal{J}$ of a polynomial of degree at least $2$ , $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{J})$ denotes the group of affine transformations that preserve $\mathcal{J}$ .

#### Lemma 5.3.

Let $f$ be a polynomial of degree at least $2$ , and let $\sigma$ be an affine transformation. Then the following statements are equivalent:

- (1) $\sigma\in\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{J}_{f})$ ;

- (2) $\mathcal{J}_{f\circ\sigma}=\mathcal{J}_{f}$ ;

- (3) $\mathcal{J}_{\sigma\circ f}=\mathcal{J}_{f}$ .

#### Proof.

Assume first that $\sigma\in\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{J}_{f})$ . Since $\sigma(\mathcal{J}_{f})=\mathcal{J}_{f}$ , the measures $\mu_{\sigma^{-1}\circ f\circ\sigma}$ and $\mu_{f}$ are equilibrium measures with the same support. Hence, $\sigma^{*}\mu_{f}=\mu_{\sigma^{-1}\circ f\circ\sigma}=\mu_{f}.$ Therefore,

$$ (f\circ\sigma)^{*}\mu_{f}=(\sigma\circ f)^{*}\mu_{f}=d\mu_{f}. $$

Applying Theorem 2.1 to $f\circ\sigma$ (or to $\sigma\circ f$ ) and measure $\rho=\mu_{f}$ , we obtain $\mu_{f\circ\sigma}=\mu_{\sigma\circ f}=\mu_{f}.$ Consequently, $\mathcal{\mathcal{J}}_{f\circ\sigma}=\mathcal{\mathcal{J}}_{\sigma\circ f}=\mathcal{\mathcal{J}}_{f}.$

Assume that $\mathcal{J}_{f\circ\sigma}=\mathcal{J}_{f}$ . Since $\mathcal{J}_{f}$ is totally invariant under $f$ and $f\circ\sigma$ , we obtain

$$ \mathcal{J}_{f}=(f\circ\sigma)^{-1}(\mathcal{J}_{f})=\sigma^{-1}(\mathcal{J}_{f}). $$

Thus $\sigma\in\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{J}_{f})$ , which completes the proof. ∎

We now prove the following rigidity result, which is the core of the proof of Theorem 1.1:

#### Theorem 5.4.

Let $k$ be a non-Archimedean field with residue characteristic $0.$ Let $f$ and $g$ be two polynomials of degree $d\geq 2$ which do not have potential good reduction. Suppose $\mathcal{J}=\mathcal{J}_{f}=\mathcal{J}_{g}$ . Then there exists $\sigma\in\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{J})$ such that $f=\sigma\circ g.$

#### Remark 5.5.

When both $f$ and $g$ have good reduction, the statement is no longer valid. For example, consider $f(z)=z^{d}$ and $g(z)=z^{d}+z.$ Both maps have good reduction, and therefore their Julia sets reduce to the Gauss point $x_{g}$ . However, there is no affine transformation $\sigma$ such that $f=\sigma\circ g.$

Before beginning the proof of Theorem 5.4, let us explain our argument when $f=z^{2}+c_{1},g=z^{2}+c_{2}$ with $|c_{i}|>1$ . In this case, choose some large $\alpha>0$ so that $\{G_{f}(z)<\alpha\}=\{G_{g}(z)<\alpha\}$ is given by a disk $D(0,R)$ . Taking preimages, we obtain that

$$ f^{-n}(D(0,R))=\left\{G_{f}(z)<\frac{\alpha}{2^{n}}\right\}=\left\{G_{g}(z)<\frac{\alpha}{2^{n}}\right\}=g^{-n}(D(0,R)). $$

Fix an $\varepsilon>0$ . We may then take $n$ large enough so that $f^{-n}(D(0,R))=g^{-n}(D(0,R))$ is a disjoint union of $2^{n}$ disks, each of radius $<\varepsilon$ . Now let $\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{2^{n}}$ be the roots of $f^{n}(z)=0$ and similarly let $\beta_{1},\ldots,\beta_{2^{n}}$ be those for $g^{n}(z)=0$ . Then we may arrange them so that $|\alpha_{i}-\beta_{i}|<\varepsilon$ for all $i$ . In particular, we obtain

$$ \sum_{1\leq i<j\leq 2^{n}}|\alpha_{i}\alpha_{j}-\beta_{i}\beta_{j}|\leq\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq 2^{n}}\left|(\alpha_{i}-\beta_{i})\alpha_{j}+(\alpha_{j}-\beta_{j})\beta_{i}\right|\leq\max\{|c_{1}|,|c_{2}|\}\varepsilon. $$

By Viète’s formulas, this implies that the coefficients of $z^{2^{n}-2}$ for $f^{n}(z)$ and $g^{n}(z)$ differ by at most $\max\{|c_{1}|,|c_{2}|\}\varepsilon$ . But this coefficient can easily be computed to be $2^{n-1}c_{1}$ and $2^{n-1}c_{2}$ . Hence

$$ |2^{n-1}||c_{1}-c_{2}|<\max\{|c_{1}|,|c_{2}|\}\varepsilon\implies|c_{1}-c_{2}|<\max\{|c_{1}|,|c_{2}|\}\varepsilon, $$

where we crucially used the fact that $k$ is of residue characteristic $0$ . Letting $\epsilon\to 0$ gives $c_{1}=c_{2}$ , proving rigidity in this case.

For general polynomials, we will use the subset $X_{v}$ for a suitable vertex $v$ , as introduced in Proposition 5.2 as a replacement for $f^{-n}(D(0,R))$ and $g^{-n}(D(0,R))$ . Keeping the notation introduced in §5.1, one has:

#### Lemma 5.6.

Let $v^{0}$ be a vertex such that the sublevel set $\{G_{f}<G_{f}(v^{0})\}$ is a disk. Then for all $\epsilon>0$ , there exists a vertex $v\in f^{-n}(v^{0})$ for some $n\in\mathbb{N}$ , such that for any $w\in Y_{v}$ , the radius of the associated ball satisfies $\mathrm{diam}(D_{w})<\epsilon.$

#### Proof.

By [50, Theorem 3.1], $f$ admits a repelling type I periodic point $p$ , which necessarily belongs to the Julia set. (Note: Although the original statement is formulated for polynomials over formal Laurent series, the proof remains valid for fields with residue characteristic $0$ . )

Up to iteration, we may assume $p$ is a fixed point. Note that $G_{f}(p)=0$ . Therefore, for any $n\in\mathbb{N}$ , there exists a unique connected component $D_{n}$ of $\{G_{f}<\frac{1}{d^{n}}G_{f}(v^{0})\}$ containing $p$ .

We claim that there exists $n$ such that $\mathrm{diam}(D_{n})<\epsilon.$ Suppose for contradiction that $\mathrm{diam}(D_{n})\geq\epsilon$ for all $n$ . Then $D(p,\epsilon)$ is contained in the intersection $\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb{N}}D_{n}$ . Since $f(\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb{N}}D_{n})=\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb{N}}D_{n}$ , we conclude that $D(p,\epsilon)$ is contained in the Fatou set of $f$ , which contradicts the fact that $p$ belongs to the Julia set. Let $v=\partial D_{n}$ . Then, $v\in f^{-n}(v^{0})$ and $\mathrm{diam}(D_{v})<\epsilon.$

Let $w\in Y_{v}$ . We claim that $v^{0}=f^{n}(v)=f^{n+1}(w)$ . This follows from the fact that $\{G_{f}<G_{f}(f^{n}(v))\}$ and $\{G_{f}<G_{f}(f^{n+1}(w))\}$ are the same disk with boundary point $v^{0}=f^{n}(v)=f^{n+1}(w)$ .

Let $h_{n}=f$ if $n$ is even and let $h_{n}=g$ if $n$ is odd. By Proposition 5.2(2), for any $w\in Y_{v}$ , there exist $s\in\mathbb{N}$ , distinct vertices $v_{0},v_{1},\dots,v_{s}=v\in X_{v}$ , and $w_{0}=w,\dots,w_{s}\in Y_{v}$ such that $h_{s}(w_{i})=v_{i}$ and $h_{s-1}(w_{i+1})=v_{i}$ . Let $e_{w_{i}}$ and $e_{v_{i}}$ denote the unique edges with lower vertices $w_{i}$ and $v_{i}$ , respectively. According to Proposition 4.7(4), we have the length relations $l(e_{v_{i}})=\deg_{w_{i}}h_{s}\cdot l(e_{w_{i}})$ and $l(e_{w_{i+1}})\leq l(e_{v_{i}})$ . Combining these yields:

$$ l(e_{v})\leq\left(\prod_{i=0}^{s}\deg_{w_{i}}h_{s}\right)\cdot l(e_{w}). $$

Note that the disks $D_{w_{i}}$ are disjoint disks. By Proposition 4.9, each disk $D_{w_{i}}$ contains exactly $\deg_{w_{i}}h_{s}-1$ critical points (counted with multiplicities). Since the total number of critical points of $h_{s}$ is $d-1$ , there are at most $d-1$ indices $i$ such that $\deg_{w_{i}}h_{s}\geq 2$ . We therefore obtain

$$ l(e_{v})\leq d^{d-1}\,l(e_{w}). $$

Let $v^{0},v^{1},\dots,v^{m}=v$ be the sequence of vertices obtained by descending along the tree to $v$ , and let $v^{0}=w^{0},w^{1},\dots,w^{m+j}=w$ be the sequence descending to $w$ . Since $w\in Y_{v}$ by assumption, it follows from Proposition 5.2(3) that $w^{i+j}\in Y_{v^{i}}$ for each $1\leq i\leq m$ . Therefore, $l(e_{v^{i}})\leq d^{d-1}l(e_{w^{i+j}})$ . Summing these lengths, we obtain:

$$ \log\frac{\mathrm{diam}(D_{v^{0}})}{\mathrm{diam}(D_{v})}=\sum_{i=1}^{m}l(e_{v^{i}})\leq d^{d-1}\sum_{i=1}^{m}l(e_{w^{i+j}})\leq d^{d-1}\log\frac{\mathrm{diam}(D_{v^{0}})}{\mathrm{diam}(D_{w})}. $$

Consequently, as $\epsilon\to 0$ , it follows that $\mathrm{diam}(D_{w})\to 0$ , which completes the proof. ∎

#### Proof of Theorem 5.4.

By Lemma 5.3, it suffices to prove that there exists an affine map $\sigma$ such that $f=\sigma\circ g$ .

Fix a vertex $v^{0}$ such that $\{G_{f}<G_{f}(v^{0})\}$ is a disk. By Lemma 5.6, for all $\epsilon>0$ , there exists a vertex $v\in f^{-n}(v^{0})$ such that for every $w\in Y_{v}$ , one has $\operatorname{diam}(D_{w})<\epsilon.$ Write $Y_{v}=\{w_{j}\}_{1\leq j\leq l}.$ By Proposition 5.2(4), there exists a finite set $A\subset\bigcup_{v_{i}\in X_{v}}D_{v_{i}}\cap k$ such that, for each $1\leq j\leq l$ , the sets $f^{-1}(A)$ and $g^{-1}(A)$ have the same cardinality in $D_{w_{j}}$ , counted with multiplicity. Since $\operatorname{diam}(D_{w_{j}})<\epsilon$ , any $x,y\in D_{w_{j}}\cap k$ satisfy $|x-y|<\epsilon$ .

Let $N=\#A$ , and write $f^{-1}(A)=\{x_{1},\dots,x_{dN}\}$ and $g^{-1}(A)=\{y_{1},\dots,y_{dN}\}$ , counted with multiplicity. After reindexing, we may assume that $|x_{i}-y_{i}|<\epsilon$ for all $1\leq i\leq dN$ . Since $x_{i},y_{i}\in D_{v^{0}}$ by construction, there exists a constant $C>0$ , independent of $\epsilon$ , such that for every $1\leq s\leq d$ , one has

$$ \left|\sum_{i=1}^{dN}x_{i}^{s}-\sum_{i=1}^{dN}y_{i}^{s}\right|\leq C\epsilon. $$

Write $f(z)=a_{d}z^{d}+a_{d-1}z^{d-1}+\cdots+a_{0},$ and $g(z)=b_{d}z^{d}+b_{d-1}z^{d-1}+\cdots+b_{0}.$ Assume that $g$ cannot be written as the composition of an affine map with $f$ . Let $i$ be the largest integer such that $\frac{a_{i}}{a_{d}}\neq\frac{b_{i}}{b_{d}}.$ Then $i\geq 1$ .

Note that for $i\geq 1$ , by Viète’s theorem, the $(d-i)$ -th elementary symmetric function of $f^{-1}(c)$ (resp. $g^{-1}(c)$ ) is independent of the choice of $c\in k$ and is equal to $\frac{a_{i}}{a_{d}}$ (resp. $\frac{b_{i}}{b_{d}}$ ). Denote by $x_{i}^{c}$ (resp. $y_{i}^{c}$ ) the preimages for $c\in A$ under $f$ (resp. $g$ ). Applying Newton’s identities and Viète’s formulas to preimages of all $c\in A$ under $f$ and $g$ , we obtain

$$ \displaystyle(-1)^{d-i}(d-i)\left(\frac{a_{i}}{a_{d}}\right) \displaystyle=(-1)^{i-1}\sum_{s=1}^{d-i}\frac{a_{i+s}}{a_{d}}\left(\sum(x_{i}^{c})^{s}\right); \displaystyle(-1)^{d-i}(d-i)\left(\frac{b_{i}}{b_{d}}\right) \displaystyle=(-1)^{i-1}\sum_{s=1}^{d-i}\frac{b_{i+s}}{b_{d}}\left(\sum(y_{i}^{c})^{s}\right). $$

Since we assume that $\frac{a_{i+s}}{a_{d}}=\frac{b_{i+s}}{b_{d}}$ , summing over all $c\in A$ and taking the difference, we obtain

$$ \displaystyle(-1)^{d-i}(d-i)N\left(\frac{a_{i}}{a_{d}}-\frac{b_{i}}{b_{d}}\right) \displaystyle=(-1)^{i-1}\sum_{s=1}^{d-i}\frac{a_{i+s}}{a_{d}}\left(\sum_{j=1}^{dN}(x_{j}^{s}-y_{j}^{s})\right). $$

Since the residue characteristic is assumed to be $0$ , we have $|(d-i)N|=1$ . It then follows from the strong triangle inequality that

$$ \left|\frac{a_{i}}{a_{d}}-\frac{b_{i}}{b_{d}}\right|\leq C\epsilon\max_{1\leq s\leq d-i}\left|\frac{a_{i+s}}{a_{d}}\right|. $$

Letting $\epsilon\to 0$ , we obtain $\frac{a_{i}}{a_{d}}=\frac{b_{i}}{b_{d}}$ , which leads to a contradiction.

Therefore, $\frac{a_{i}}{a_{d}}=\frac{b_{i}}{b_{d}}$ for all $i\geq 1$ . Let $\lambda=\frac{a_{d}}{b_{d}}$ and $\mu=a_{0}-\frac{b_{0}a_{d}}{b_{d}}$ , then $f=\lambda g+\mu$ , which proves the claim. ∎

### 5.3. Group of dynamical symmetries

We recall from [42, §3] the notion of the dynamical symmetry group of a polynomial over a field $k$ with characteristic $0$ .

We begin with monic and centered polynomials. A reduced presentation of $f\in k[z]$ is a decomposition

$$ f(z)=z^{\mu}f_{0}(z^{m}), $$

where $\mu,m\geq 0$ , $f_{0}(0)\neq 0$ , and $f_{0}$ is not of the form $h(z^{l})$ for any polynomial $h$ with $\deg h\geq 1$ and any $l\geq 2$ . Such a presentation is unique.

The group of dynamical symmetries of $f$ , denoted by $\Sigma_{f}$ , is defined by

$$ \Sigma_{f}=\begin{cases}\mathbb{U}_{m},&\text{if }f_{0}\neq 1,\\
\bigcup_{m=1}^{\infty}\mathbb{U}_{m},&\text{if }f_{0}=1,\end{cases} $$

where $\mathbb{U}_{m}$ denotes the cyclic group of $m$ -th roots of unity.

Now let $f$ be an arbitrary polynomial of degree at least $2$ , and let $L$ be an affine transformation such that $L^{-1}\circ f\circ L$ is monic and centered. We define the group of dynamical symmetries of $f$ by

$$ \Sigma_{f}=\bigl\{L^{-1}\circ\sigma\circ L\big|\sigma\in\Sigma_{L^{-1}\circ f\circ L}\bigr\}. $$

This definition is independent of the choice of the affine transformation $M$ .

A priori, the dynamical symmetry group $\Sigma_{f}$ is defined in purely algebraic terms. However, as a consequence of rigidity phenomena for complex Julia sets, Favre–Gauthier [42, Proposition 3.9] proved $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{J}_{f})=\Sigma_{f}$ when $f$ is not a monomial.

#### Proposition 5.7.

Let $f$ be a complex polynomial of degree $d\geq 2$ . Then:

- (1) The group $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{J}_{f})$ of affine transformations preserving $\mathcal{J}_{f}$ coincides with the group of all $\sigma\in\mathrm{Aff}(\mathbb{C})$ such that the Green function satisfies $G_{f}(\sigma(z))=G_{f}(z).$

- (2) If $f$ is not conjugate to the monomial $M_{d}(z)=z^{d}$ , then $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{J}_{f})=\Sigma_{f}.$ Otherwise, $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{J}_{M_{d}})=\mathbb{S}^{1}$ , whereas $\Sigma_{M_{d}}$ is the group of roots of unity.

Following the same philosophy, we establish an analogous comparison between $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{J}_{f})$ and $\Sigma_{f}$ in the non-Archimedean setting. This will follow from Theorem 5.4.

#### Proposition 5.8.

Let $k$ be a non-Archimedean field with residue characteristic $0$ . Let $f(z)\in k[z]$ be a polynomial of degree at least $2$ .

- (1) The group $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{J}_{f})$ coincides with the group of $\sigma\in\mathrm{Aff}(k)$ such that the Green function satisfies $G_{f}(\sigma(z))=G_{f}(z)$ ;

- (2) Suppose $f$ has potential good reduction. Let $L\in\mathrm{Aff}(k)$ such that $L(\mathcal{J}_{f})=x_{g}$ , then

$$ \mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{J}_{f})=\{L^{-1}\circ(az+b)\circ L\mid|a|=1,|b|\leq 1\}. $$

- (3) If $f$ does not have potential good reduction, then

$$ \mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{J}_{f})=\Sigma_{f}. $$

#### Proof.

(1) Let $\sigma\in\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{J}_{f})$ . Then $\mathcal{J}_{\sigma^{-1}\circ f\circ\sigma}=\sigma^{-1}(\mathcal{J}_{f})=\mathcal{J}_{f}.$ By [3, Theorem 10.91], we have $G_{\sigma^{-1}\circ f\circ\sigma}(z)=G_{f}(z).$ It follows from Proposition 4.3(4) that

$$ G_{f}(\sigma(z))=G_{\sigma^{-1}\circ f\circ\sigma}(z)=G_{f}(z). $$

Conversely, suppose $\sigma\in\mathrm{Aff}(k)$ satisfies $G_{f}(\sigma(z))=G_{f}(z)$ for all $z$ . Then $\sigma$ preserves the filled-in Julia set $\cal{K}_{f}$ , and hence also its boundary, $\mathcal{J}_{f}=\partial\cal{K}_{f}.$ Therefore, $\sigma\in\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{J}_{f})$ .

(2) The second statement follows from the observation that the group of affine transformations fixing $x_{g}$ is precisely $\{az+b\mid|a|=1,|b|\leq 1\}$ .

(3) Up to conjugation, we may assume that $f$ is monic and centered, and write its reduced presentation as $f(z)=z^{\mu}f_{0}(z^{m}).$

By Lemma 5.3, for any $\sigma\in\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{J}_{f})$ we have $\mathcal{J}_{f\circ\sigma}=\mathcal{J}_{f}.$ By Theorem 5.4, there exists an element $\rho(\sigma)\in\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{J}_{f})$ such that

$$ f\circ\sigma=\rho(\sigma)\circ f. $$

Moreover, the map $\rho\colon\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{J}_{f})\longrightarrow\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{J}_{f})$ is a group homomorphism.

We claim that $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{J}_{f})$ is finite. Assuming this claim, it then follows from [42, Proposition 3.6] that $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{J}_{f})\subseteq\Sigma_{f}.$

Conversely, let $\lambda\in\mathbb{U}_{m}=\Sigma_{f}$ . A direct computation shows that

$$ (\lambda f)^{k}(z)=\lambda^{1+\mu+\cdots+\mu^{k-1}}f^{k}(z)\quad\text{for all }k\geq 1. $$

Hence the associated Green functions satisfy $G_{\lambda f}=G_{f},$ which implies $\mathcal{J}_{\lambda f}=\mathcal{J}_{f}.$ By Lemma 5.3, we conclude that $\lambda z\in\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{J}_{f})$ . Therefore, $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{J}_{f})=\Sigma_{f}.$

It remains to prove the claim that $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{J}_{f})$ is finite. By (5.1), each $\sigma\in\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{J}_{f})$ permutes the critical points of $f$ . Since an affine transformation is uniquely determined by the images of two distinct points, it follows that if $f$ has at least two critical points, then $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{J}_{f})$ is finite.

If instead $f$ is unicritical, then, since $f$ is monic, centered, and has bad reduction, it can be written as $f(z)=z^{d}+C$ with $C\in k^{\times}.$ In this case, $\sigma$ fixes the unique critical point $0$ , and hence must be of the form $\sigma(z)=\lambda z$ for some $\lambda\in k^{\times}$ . Similarly, we may write $\rho(\sigma)(z)=\lambda^{\prime}z$ . Then (5.1) gives $(\lambda z)^{d}+C=\lambda^{\prime}(z^{d}+C).$ It follows that $\lambda$ is a root of unity and $\lambda^{\prime}=1$ . Hence $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{J}_{f})$ is finite in this case as well. ∎

### 5.4. General rigidity of Julia sets

In order to prove Theorem 1.1, we need the following rigidity theorem for complex polynomials.

Recall that $k$ is an algebraically closed field of characteristic $0$ , and let

$$ f(z)=a_{d}z^{d}+a_{d-1}z^{d-1}+\cdots $$

be a polynomial of degree $d\geq 2$ over $k$ . A formal series $\phi_{f}\in k[[z^{-1}]][z]$ is called a Böttcher coordinate if it satisfies

$$ \phi_{f}\circ f=\phi_{f}^{d}, $$

see [84, §9] and [42, §2.5].

In fact, $\phi_{f}$ can be written in the form

$$ \phi_{f}=\alpha\left(z+\frac{a_{d-1}}{da_{d}}\right)+\sum_{j\geq 1}\alpha_{j}z^{-j}, $$

where $\alpha^{\,d-1}=a_{d}$ and $\alpha_{j}\in\mathbb{Q}(a_{i},\alpha)$ . Moreover, $\phi_{f}$ is uniquely determined up to multiplication by a $(d-1)$ -st root of unity.

#### Theorem 5.9.

Assume that $\mathcal{J}$ is the Julia set of a complex polynomial of degree at least $2$ which is not integrable. Let $g$ be a polynomial of minimal degree whose Julia set equals $\mathcal{J}$ .

For any complex polynomial $f$ of degree $d\geq 2$ , the following conditions are equivalent:

- (1) There exist an integer $n\geq 1$ and $\sigma\in\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{J})$ such that $f=\sigma\circ g^{n}.$

- (2) The Julia sets coincide: $\mathcal{J}_{f}=\mathcal{J}.$

- (3) The equilibrium measures coincide: $\mu_{f}=\mu_{g}.$

- (4) The Green functions coincide: $G_{f}=G_{g}.$

- (5) The Böttcher coordinates at $\infty$ agree up to a root of unity: $\phi_{f}=\lambda\phi_{g}$ , where $\lambda$ is a root of unity.

#### Proof.

The equivalence of (1) and (2) was proved by Schmidt–Steinmetz [93]. For the equivalence of (2), (3), and (4), we refer the reader to [90]. The implication (5) $\Rightarrow$ (4) follows from the identity $G_{f}=\log|\phi_{f}|=\log|\phi_{g}|=G_{g},$ see [84, §9].

It remains to prove that (1) and (4) imply (5). Since $\log|\phi_{f}|=\log|\phi_{g}|$ , there exists $\lambda\in\mathbb{S}^{1}$ such that $\phi_{f}=\lambda\phi_{g}.$ Up to conjugation, we may assume that $f$ is monic and centered. Write

$$ \phi_{f}(z)=z+\cdots,\qquad\phi_{g}(z)=\frac{1}{\lambda}z+\cdots. $$

By Proposition 5.7, $\sigma$ is given by multiplication by a root of unity. Moreover, $\sigma(z)=\lambda^{d-1}z$ : indeed, the leading coefficient of $g^{n}=\sigma^{-1}\circ f$ is the $(d-1)$ st power of the leading coefficient $\lambda$ of the Böttcher coordinate $\phi_{g}=\phi_{g^{n}}$ . It follows that $\lambda^{d-1}$ is a root of unity, and hence $\lambda$ itself is a root of unity. ∎

#### Lemma 5.10.

Let $k$ be a non-Archimedean field with residue characteristic $0.$ Let $f\in k[z]$ be a polynomial of degree at least $2$ which does not have potential good reduction. Suppose $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{J}_{f})=\{\lambda z\in\mathrm{Aff}(k)\mid\lambda\in\mathbb{U}_{m}\}$ . Then there exist an integer $\mu\geq 0$ and a polynomial $f_{0}\in k[z]$ such that $f(z)=z^{\mu}f_{0}(z^{m}).$

#### Proof.

If $m=1$ , the conclusion is immediate. We therefore assume that $m\neq 1$ .

Let $L$ be an affine transformation such that $L^{-1}\circ f\circ L$ is monic and centered. Let $L^{-1}\circ f\circ L(z)=z^{\mu}h_{0}(z^{m_{1}})$ be a reduced representation, where $h_{0}(z)=\sum_{i=0}^{\delta}a_{i}z^{i}.$

Applying Proposition 5.8 to $L^{-1}\circ f\circ L$ , we obtain

$$ \mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{J}_{f})=\{L\circ\sigma\circ L^{-1}\in\mathrm{Aff}(k)\mid\text{
$\sigma(z)=\lambda z$ for some
$\lambda\in\mathbb{U}_{m_{1}}$}\}. $$

Since $\#\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{J}_{f})=m$ by assumption, it follows that $m=m_{1}$ . Thus $L\circ\mathbb{U}_{m}\circ L^{-1}=\mathbb{U}_{m}.$ Hence $L$ is of the form $L(z)=az.$ Define $f_{0}(z)=\sum_{i=0}^{\delta}a_{i}a^{im+\mu-1}z^{i}.$ Then we have

$$ f(z)=z^{\mu}f_{0}(z^{m}), $$

which proves the desired decomposition. ∎

#### Lemma 5.11.

Let $k$ be a non-Archimedean field of residue characteristic $0$ , and let $K\subseteq k$ be a subfield. Let $f\in K[z]$ be a polynomial of degree at least $2$ . Suppose that $f$ does not have potential good reduction.

Then for any embedding $\jmath:K/\mathbb{Q}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{C}/\mathbb{Q},$ we have

$$ \jmath\big(\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{J}_{f})\big)=\mathrm{Aut}\big(\mathcal{J}_{\jmath(f)}\big). $$

#### Proof.

Since $f$ does not have potential good reduction, $\jmath(f)$ is not conjugate to a monomial. Therefore, by Proposition 5.7 and 5.8, one obtains

$$ \jmath(\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{J}_{f}))=\jmath(\Sigma_{f})=\Sigma_{\jmath(f)}=\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{J}_{\jmath(f)}), $$

which completes the proof. ∎

#### Theorem 1.1.

Let $k$ be an algebraically closed, complete non-Archimedean field with residue characteristic $0$ . Let $\mathcal{J}$ be the Julia set of a polynomial of degree at least $2$ which does not have potential good reduction. Let $g$ be a polynomial of minimal degree whose Julia set coincides with $\mathcal{J}$ .

For any polynomial $f$ of degree $d\geq 2$ , the following conditions are equivalent:

- (1) There exist an integer $n\geq 1$ and $\sigma\in\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{J})$ such that $f=\sigma\circ g^{n}.$

- (2) The Julia sets coincide: $\mathcal{J}_{f}=\mathcal{J}.$

- (3) The equilibrium measures coincide: $\mu_{f}=\mu_{g}.$

- (4) The Green functions coincide: $G_{f}=G_{g}.$

- (5) The Böttcher coordinates at $\infty$ agree up to a root of unity: $\phi_{f}=\lambda\phi_{g}$ , where $\lambda$ is a root of unity.

#### Proof.

The equivalence of (3) and (4) follows from [46, Section 4] and the equivalence of (2) and (3) follows from [3, Theorem 10.91]. Assume (1) holds, then Lemma 5.3 implies that $\mathcal{J}_{f}=\mathcal{J}_{g}.$ Also, by Lemma 5.11, one has

$$ \jmath(f)=\jmath(\sigma)\circ\jmath(g)^{n} $$

with $\jmath(\sigma)\in\mathrm{Aut}(\cal{J}_{\jmath(g)}).$ By Theorem 5.9, the Böttcher coordinates $\phi_{\jmath(f)}$ and $\phi_{\jmath(g)}$ coincide up to multiplication by a root of unity. Consequently the same holds for $\phi_{f}$ and $\phi_{g}$ .

Next we prove (5) implies (1). Let $K$ be a field finitely generated over $\mathbb{Q}$ such that $f,g,\phi_{f},$ and $\phi_{g}$ are defined over $K$ . Let $\jmath\colon K/\mathbb{Q}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{C}/\mathbb{Q}$ be an embedding. Since $g$ does not have potential good reduction, $\jmath(g)$ is not conjugate to a monomial.

If $\phi_{f}=\lambda\phi_{g}$ for some root of unity $\lambda$ , then $\phi_{\jmath(f)}=\lambda\phi_{\jmath(g)}$ . By Theorem 5.9, there exists a polynomial $Q\in\mathbb{C}[z]$ such that

$$ \jmath(f)=\sigma_{1}\circ Q^{l_{1}},\qquad\jmath(g)=\sigma_{2}\circ Q^{l_{2}}, $$

for some $\sigma_{i}\in\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{J}_{\jmath(g)})$ and integers $l_{i}\geq 1$ . Therefore,

$$ f=\jmath^{-1}(\sigma_{1})\circ\jmath^{-1}(Q)^{l_{1}},\qquad g=\jmath^{-1}(\sigma_{2})\circ\jmath(Q)^{l_{2}}, $$

By Lemma 5.11, one has $j^{-1}(\sigma_{i})\in\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{J}).$ It then follows from Lemma 5.3 that

$$ \mathcal{J}_{f}=\mathcal{J}_{g}=\mathcal{J}_{\jmath^{-1}(Q)}. $$

Since $g$ was chosen to have minimal degree, we must have $\deg g=\deg Q$ . Consequently $\deg f=\deg(g^{\,l_{1}})$ . Applying Theorem 5.4 to $f$ and $g^{l_{1}}$ yields

$$ f=\sigma\circ g^{\,l_{1}} $$

for some $\sigma\in\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{J})$ .

It remains to prove (3) implies (5). We may assume that $f$ is monic and centered. Let $f(z)=z^{\mu}f_{0}(z^{m})$ be a reduced representation. By Proposition 5.8(3), $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{J})=\{\lambda z\in\mathrm{Aff}(k)\mid\lambda\in\mathbb{U}_{m}\}$ for some $m\in\mathbb{Z}$ .

Note that $(f\circ g)^{*}(\mu_{f})=\deg(f\circ g)\mu_{f}.$ By Theorem 2.1, we obtain $\mu_{f\circ g}=\mu_{g}$ , and hence $\mathcal{J}_{f\circ g}=\mathcal{J}.$ Similarly, $\mathcal{J}_{g\circ f}=\mathcal{J}$ . Applying Theorem 5.4 to $f\circ g$ and $g\circ f$ , we deduce that there exists $\zeta\in\mathbb{U}_{m}$ such that

$$ f\circ g=\zeta g\circ f. $$

By Lemma 5.10, we may write $g(z)=z^{\nu}g_{0}(z^{m}).$ Define $\hat{f}(z)=z^{\mu}(f_{0}(z))^{m},$ and $\hat{g}(z)=z^{\nu}(g_{0}(z))^{m}.$ Then (5.2) implies

$$ \hat{f}\circ\hat{g}=\hat{g}\circ\hat{f}. $$

Thus $\jmath(\hat{f})$ and $\jmath(\hat{g})$ commute. By the classical results of Julia [69], Fatou [41], Ritt [91], one of the following occurs.

(1) $\jmath(\hat{f})$ is a monomial, or $\pm\jmath(\hat{f})$ is conjugate to a Chebyshev polynomial. In this case $f$ would also be conjugate to a Chebyshev polynomial, which has potential good reduction, contradicting our assumption.

(2) There exist integers $n_{1},n_{2}\geq 1$ such that $\jmath(\hat{f}^{n_{1}})=\jmath(\hat{g}^{n_{2}}).$ Since $\deg\hat{f}=\deg f$ and $\deg\hat{g}=\deg g$ , this implies

$$ \deg(f^{n_{1}})=\deg(g^{n_{2}}). $$

Applying Theorem 5.4 to the iterates $f^{n_{1}}$ and $g^{n_{2}}$ , we obtain some $\zeta^{\prime}\in\mathbb{U}_{m}$ such that $f^{n_{1}}=\zeta^{\prime}g^{n_{2}}.$ Applying the implication $(1)\Rightarrow(5)$ to $\zeta^{\prime}g^{n_{2}}$ , we then get

$$ \phi_{f}=\phi_{\zeta^{\prime}g^{n_{2}}}=\lambda\phi_{g} $$

for some root of unity $\lambda$ . This proves the statement. ∎

## 6. Uniform bounds on common preperiodic points

In this section, we will prove Theorem 1.2.

We will follow the strategy of DeMarco–Krieger–Ye [29, 30].

Let $f,g\in K[z]$ be polynomials of degrees $d_{1},d_{2}\geq 2$ , respectively, defined over a number field $K$ . Suppose further that $f$ is monic and centered. For each place $\nu\in M_{K}$ , we may define a local energy pairing

$$ \langle f,g\rangle_{\nu}=-\iint_{\mathbb{P}_{\nu}^{1,\mathrm{an}}\times\mathbb{P}_{\nu}^{1,\mathrm{an}}}\log|x-y|_{\nu}d(\mu_{f,\nu}-\mu_{g,\nu})(x)d(\mu_{f,\nu}-\mu_{g,\nu})(y). $$

We can then define a global energy pairing by

$$ \langle f,g\rangle=\sum_{\nu\in M_{K}}N_{\nu}\langle f,g\rangle_{\nu} $$

where $N_{\nu}=\frac{[K_{\nu}:\mathbb{Q}_{p}]}{[K:\mathbb{Q}]}$ . Let $h(f),h(g)$ be the standard Weil heights on the coefficients of $f$ and $g$ . Then to establish Theorem 1.2, we have to prove the existence of constants $c_{1},c_{2}>0$ , depending only on $d_{1}$ and $d_{2}$ , so that

$$ \langle f,g\rangle\geq c_{1}(h(f)+h(g))+c_{2}. $$

This would follow from suitable uniform lower bounds on the local energy pairing $\langle f,g\rangle_{\nu}$ , which in turn would follow from Theorem 1.1 using a degeneration argument.

### 6.1. Uniform bounds for local pairings

We will begin by proving uniform lower bounds for $\langle f,g\rangle_{\nu}$ .

Write $f=\sum_{i=0}^{d_{1}}a_{i}z^{i}$ and $g=\sum_{i=0}^{d_{2}}b_{i}z^{i}$ . Recall the following notation: $|f|=\max\{|a_{i}|\}$ ; $|(f,g)|=\max\{|a_{i}|,|b_{j}|,|b_{d_{2}}|^{-1}\}$ ;

$$ |\operatorname{Res}(f)|=\frac{|a_{d}|^{d}}{\max_{0\leq i\leq d}\{1,|a_{i}|\}^{2d}}; $$

and

$$ \epsilon(f_{n})=\bigl(-\log(|\operatorname{Res}(f_{n})|/C_{d})\bigr)^{-1}, $$

where $C_{d}=e\,\sup_{\mathrm{Rat}_{d}(\mathbb{C})}|\operatorname{Res}|$ if $k_{n}=\mathbb{C}$ , and $C_{d}=1$ otherwise.

#### Lemma 6.1.

Let $k$ be a non-Archimedean field with residue characteristic $0$ . Let $f$ be a monic centered polynomial of degree $d\geq 2$ . Then $f$ has good reduction if and only if $f$ has potential good reduction.

#### Proof.

The implication “good reduction $\Rightarrow$ potential good reduction” is obvious. We prove the converse.

Write $f(z)=z^{d}+a_{d-2}z^{d-2}+\cdots+a_{0}.$ Assume that $f$ has potential good reduction. Then there exists a type II fixed point $x=\zeta(a,R)$ with local degree $d$ . Let $M(z)=\lambda z+a$ with $|\lambda|=R$ . Define $g=M^{-1}\circ f\circ M.$ A direct computation shows that $g(z)=\lambda^{d-1}z^{d}+da\lambda^{d-2}z^{d-1}+\cdots.$

Since $\tilde{g}$ has degree $d$ , we conclude $|\lambda|^{d-1}=1,$ and $|da\lambda^{d-2}|\leq 1.$ Because the residue characteristic of $k$ is $0$ , we have $|d|=1$ , and therefore $|a|\leq 1.$ It follows that $x=\zeta(0,1)$ , and hence $f$ has good reduction. ∎

Let $V$ be a Zariski-closed subvariety of $\mathrm{Poly}_{\mathrm{mc}}^{d_{1}}$ of positive dimension. Then by [42, Proposition 3.9], there exists a positive integer $m\geq 1$ and a proper subvariety $V^{\prime}\subset V$ such that for all $f\in(V\setminus V^{\prime})(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$ , the group of dynamical symmetries is $\mathbb{U}_{m}$ . We can describe explicit equations cutting out $V^{\prime}$ as follows.

For any positive integer $m$ , let $V_{m}$ be the set of monic centered polynomials $f(z)=z^{d_{1}}+\sum_{i=0}^{d_{1}-2}a_{i}z^{i}$ such that $m\mid\#\Sigma_{f}.$ Then

$$ V_{m}=\bigcup_{m\mid d_{1}-\mu}\left\{a_{i}=0\;\middle|\;m\nmid(i-\mu)\right\} $$

defines a Zariski closed subvariety of $\mathrm{Poly}_{\mathrm{mc}}^{d_{1}}.$ Set $V^{\prime}=(\bigcup_{m^{\prime}\nmid m}V_{m^{\prime}})\cup(\bigcup_{i\geq 1}V_{im}).$ Then $V^{\prime}$ is a Zariski-closed subvariety defined by finitely many monomials $p_{1},\dots,p_{\ell}$ .

For any metrized field $k$ of characteristic $0$ and any $f\in k[z]$ , we define

$$ \lambda_{V^{\prime},k}(f)=-\log\max\{|p_{1}(f)|,\dots,|p_{\ell}(f)|\}. $$

Then $\lambda_{V^{\prime},k}=+\infty$ if and only if $f\in V^{\prime}(k)$ .

By construction, we have that $f\in(V\setminus V^{\prime})(k)$ if and only if $\Sigma_{f}=\mathbb{U}_{m}.$

#### Theorem 1.6.

Let $(k,|\cdot|)$ be a field of characteristic $0$ equipped with a nontrivial absolute value, and fix $C_{1},C_{2}>0$ . Then there exist constants $C_{3},C_{4}>0$ depending only on $k$ such that the following holds:

Suppose that

$$ (f,g)\in(V\setminus V^{\prime})(k)\times\operatorname{Poly}^{d_{2}}(k) $$

satisfies

$$ \lambda_{V^{\prime}}(f)\leq C_{1}\log|(f,g)|. $$

If positive integers $n_{1},n_{2}$ exist with $d_{1}^{n_{1}}=d_{2}^{n_{2}}$ , assume further that

$$ \log|f^{n_{1}}-\lambda g^{n_{2}}|\geq-C_{2}\log|(f,g)|\quad\text{for all }\lambda\in\mathbb{U}_{m}. $$

Then

$$ \log|(f,g)|\geq C_{3}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\langle f,g\rangle\geq C_{4}\log|(f,g)|. $$

#### Proof.

We argue by contradiction. Suppose that there exists a sequence $(f_{n},g_{n})\in V\setminus V^{\prime}\times\mathrm{Poly}^{d_{2}}(k)$ such that, upon setting

$$ \epsilon_{n}:=\Bigl(\log|(f_{n},g_{n})|\Bigr)^{-1}, $$

the following properties hold:

- (1) $\lambda_{V^{\prime},k}(f_{n})\leq C_{1}\epsilon_{n}^{-1}$ ;

- (2) $\log|f_{n}^{n_{1}}-\lambda g_{n}^{n_{2}}|\geq-C_{2}\epsilon_{n}^{-1}$ for all $\lambda\in\mathbb{U}_{m}$ ;

- (3) $\epsilon_{n}^{-1}\geq n$ ;

- (4) $\langle f_{n},g_{n}\rangle\leq\frac{1}{n}\epsilon_{n}^{-1}$ .

By construction, $\lim_{n\to\infty}\epsilon_{n}=0$ .

Fix a non-principal ultrafilter $\omega$ . By Proposition 3.2, the field

$$ \mathscr{H}(\omega)=\Bigl\{(z_{n})\in k^{\mathbb{N}}\bigm|\lim_{\omega}|z_{n}|^{\epsilon_{n}}<\infty\Bigr\}\Big/\Bigl\{(z_{n})\in k^{\mathbb{N}}\bigm|\lim_{\omega}|z_{n}|^{\epsilon_{n}}=0\Bigr\} $$

is a non-Archimedean field. Moreover, for any integer $m$ we have $\lim_{\omega}|m|^{\epsilon_{n}}=1.$ It follows that the residue field of $\mathscr{H}(\omega)$ has characteristic $0$ .

By construction, the sequences $(f_{n})$ and $(g_{n})$ induce polynomial maps $f_{\omega}$ and $g_{\omega}$ of degrees $d_{1}$ and $d_{2}$ , respectively, over $\mathscr{H}(\omega)$ . Moreover,

$$ \displaystyle\max\{|a_{i,\omega}|,|b_{j,\omega}|,|b_{d_{2},\omega}|^{-1}|\}=e. $$

Passing to the ultralimit, we obtain $\lambda_{V^{\prime},\mathscr{H}(\omega)}(f_{\omega})\leq C_{1}<\infty$ and $\log|f_{\omega}^{n_{1}}-\lambda g_{\omega}^{n_{2}}|\geq-C_{2}>-\infty$ . Thus we have

$$ \displaystyle\Sigma_{f}=\mathbb{U}_{m},~\text{and $f_{\omega}^{n_{1}}\neq\lambda g_{\omega}^{n_{2}}$ for all
$\lambda\in\mathbb{U}_{m}$.} $$

Furthermore, by Theorem 3.8, one has $\langle f_{\omega},g_{\omega}\rangle=\lim_{\omega}\epsilon_{n}\langle f_{n},g_{n}\rangle=0.$ It then follows from [46, Proposition 4.5] that $\mu_{f_{\omega}}=\mu_{g_{\omega}}$ . Hence $\mathcal{J}_{f_{\omega}}=\mathcal{J}_{g_{\omega}}.$ In particular, $f_{\omega}$ has good reduction if and only if $g_{\omega}$ has good reduction. If so, $\max\{|a_{i,\omega},|b_{j,\omega}|,|b_{d_{2},\omega}|^{-1}|\}=1$ , which contradicts (6.2). Hence, both $f_{\omega}$ and $g_{\omega}$ does not have good reduction.

Since $f_{\omega}$ is monic and centered, Lemma 6.1 implies that $f_{\omega}$ does not have potential good reduction. Therefore, by Theorem 5.4 and Proposition 5.8(3), there exists $\lambda\in\mathbb{U}_{m}$ such that $f_{\omega}^{n_{1}}=\lambda g_{\omega}^{n_{2}},$ which contradicts (6.3). ∎

The proof of Theorem 1.7 follows the same lines as that of Theorem 1.6, with only minor modifications.

#### Theorem 1.7.

For every $C_{1},C_{2}>0$ , there exist constants $C_{5},C_{6}>0$ depending only on $d_{1}$ and $d_{2}$ such that the following holds: Let $(k,|\cdot|)$ be a non-Archimedean field whose residue characteristic is at least $C_{5}$ , and let

$$ (f,g)\in(V\setminus V^{\prime})\times\operatorname{Poly}^{d_{2}}(k) $$

satisfy

$$ \lambda_{V^{\prime},k}(f)\leq C_{1}\log|(f,g)|. $$

Suppose moreover that whenever there exist positive integers $n_{1},n_{2}$ with

$$ d_{1}^{n_{1}}=d_{2}^{n_{2}}, $$

the following additional condition is imposed:

$$ \log|f^{n_{1}}-\lambda g^{n_{2}}|\geq-C_{2}\log|(f,g)|\qquad\text{for every }\lambda\in\mathbb{U}_{m}. $$

Then

$$ \langle f,g\rangle\geq C_{6}\log|(f,g)|. $$

#### Proof of Theorem 1.7.

For the sake of contradiction, we obtain a sequence of fields $(k_{n},|\cdot|_{n})$ with residue characteristic at least $n$ , and a sequence $(f_{n},g_{n})\subset V\setminus V^{\prime}\times\mathrm{Poly}^{d_{2}}(k_{n})$ . Setting

$$ \epsilon_{n}:=\Bigl(\log|(f_{n},g_{n})|_{n}\Bigr)^{-1}, $$

one has

- (1) $\lambda_{V^{\prime},k_{n}}(f_{n})\leq C_{1}\epsilon_{n}^{-1}$ ;

- (2) $\log|f_{n}^{n_{1}}-\lambda g_{n}^{n_{2}}|_{n}\geq-C_{2}\epsilon_{n}^{-1}$ for all $\lambda\in\mathbb{U}_{m}$ ;

- (3) $\langle f_{n},g_{n}\rangle<\frac{1}{n}\epsilon_{n}^{-1}$ .

By Proposition 3.2, the field

$$ \mathscr{H}(\omega)=\left\{(z_{n})\in\prod_{n\in\mathbb{N}}k_{n}\mid\lim_{\omega}|z_{n}|_{n}^{\epsilon_{n}}<\infty\right\}/\left\{(z_{n})\in\prod_{n\in\mathbb{N}}k_{n}\mid\lim_{\omega}|z_{n}|_{n}^{\epsilon_{n}}=0\right\} $$

is a non-Archimedean field. Since we have assumed $\mathrm{char}(\tilde{k}_{n})\geq n$ , for any fixed integer $a$ , $\lim_{\omega}|a|_{n}^{\epsilon_{n}}=1$ . Therefore, $\mathscr{H}(\omega)$ has residue characteristic $0$ .

As in the proof of Theorem 1.6, $f_{\omega}$ and $g_{\omega}$ are maps of degrees $d_{1}$ and $d_{2}$ , respectively; at least one of them does not have good reduction, and

$$ \mathrm{Aut}(f_{\omega})=\mathbb{U}_{m},\qquad f_{\omega}^{n_{1}}\neq\lambda g_{\omega}^{n_{2}}~\text{for all }\lambda\in\mathbb{U}_{m},\qquad\mu_{f_{\omega}}=\mu_{g_{\omega}}. $$

The equality of equilibrium measures implies that neither $f_{\omega}$ nor $g_{\omega}$ has good reduction. By Lemma 6.1, it follows that neither map has potential good reduction. Applying Theorem 5.4, we obtain a contradiction. ∎

### 6.2. Uniform bounds for global energy pairings

We now begin the proof of (6.1).

#### 6.2.1. Places and height

We refer the reader to [59] for a general reference.

Let $M_{\mathbb{Q}}$ denote the set consisting of all prime numbers together with the symbol $\infty$ . We write $|\cdot|_{\infty}$ for the usual absolute value on $\mathbb{Q}$ , and for each prime number $p$ we denote by $|\cdot|_{p}$ the $p$ -adic norm, normalized so that $|p|_{p}=p^{-1}$ .

Let $K$ be a number field, that is, a finite extension of $\mathbb{Q}$ . We define $M_{K}$ to be the set of all multiplicative norms on $K$ extending one of the absolute values $|\cdot|_{\nu}$ with $\nu\in M_{\mathbb{Q}}$ . Elements of $M_{K}$ are called places of $K$ . For each $\nu\in M_{K}$ , we denote by $|\cdot|_{\nu}$ the corresponding multiplicative norm on $K$ . A place $\nu$ is said to be Archimedean if its restriction to $\mathbb{Q}$ coincides with $|\cdot|_{\infty}$ , and non-Archimedean otherwise.

Each place $\nu$ gives rise to a local field. More precisely, let $K_{\nu}$ be the completion of $K$ with respect to $|\cdot|_{\nu}$ , and let $\mathbb{Q}_{\nu}$ be the closure of $\mathbb{Q}$ inside $K_{\nu}$ . We denote by $\mathbb{C}_{\nu}$ the completion of an algebraic closure of $K_{\nu}$ . The field $\mathbb{C}_{\nu}$ is then complete and algebraically closed. Moreover, for every Archimedean place $\nu$ (denoted by $\nu\mid\infty$ ), one has an isomorphism $\mathbb{C}_{\nu}\simeq\mathbb{C}$ ; and for every non-Archimedean place $\nu$ over $p$ (denoted by $\nu\mid p$ ), one has an isomorphism $\mathbb{C}_{\nu}\simeq\mathbb{C}_{p}$ .

Equivalently, a place $\nu\in M_{K}$ extending a place $v\in M_{\mathbb{Q}}$ can be described by an embedding $\sigma_{\nu}\colon K\hookrightarrow\mathbb{C}_{v}$ such that $|a|_{\nu}=|\sigma_{\nu}(a)|_{v},$ for all $a\in K$ .

We associate to each place $\nu\in M_{K}$ the weight $N_{\nu}:=\frac{[K_{\nu}:\mathbb{Q}_{\nu}]}{[K:\mathbb{Q}]}.$ A fundamental fact is that for every $\alpha\in K^{\ast}$ , all but finitely many places $\nu\in M_{K}$ satisfy $|\alpha|_{\nu}=1$ , and the following product formula holds:

$$ \prod_{\nu\in M_{K}}|\alpha|_{\nu}^{N_{\nu}}=1. $$

This leads naturally to the notion of height. For $\alpha\in K$ , we define its height by

$$ h(\alpha):=\sum_{\nu\in M_{K}}N_{\nu}\log^{+}|\alpha|_{\nu}. $$

By the product formula, one has $h(\alpha)=h(\alpha^{-1})$ for $\alpha\neq 0$ . Moreover, this definition is independent of the choice of the number field $K$ containing $\alpha$ .

Recall that $|f|_{\nu}=\max\{|a_{i}|_{\nu}\}$ and $|(f,g)|_{\nu}=\max\bigl\{|a_{i}|_{\nu},|b_{j}|_{\nu},|b_{d_{2}}|_{\nu}^{-1}\bigr\}.$ We define the height for polynomials and polynomial pairs:

$$ \displaystyle h(f) \displaystyle:=\sum_{\nu\in M_{K}}N_{\nu}\,\log^{+}|f|_{\nu}. \displaystyle h(f,g) \displaystyle:=\sum_{\nu\in M_{K}}N_{\nu}\,\log^{+}|(f,g)|_{\nu}. $$

Similarly, the definitions do not depend on the choice of $K.$

We shall use the following lemma in the sequel.

#### Lemma 6.2.

Let $f,g$ be two polynomials (possibly constant) defined over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ . Then

- (1) $h(f,g)\leq h(f)+2h(g)\leq 3h(f,g)$ ;

- (2) $h(f+g)\leq h(f)+h(g)+\log 2$

- (3) Fix two positive integers $n_{1}$ and $n_{2}$ . Then there exists a constant $R=R(n_{1},n_{2})>2$ such that

$$ h(f^{n_{1}},g^{n_{2}})\leq Rh(f,g)+R $$

#### Proof.

Note that

$$ \displaystyle h(f,g) \displaystyle=\sum_{\nu\in M_{K}}N_{\nu}\,\log\max\{|a_{i}|_{\nu},|b_{j}|_{\nu},|b_{d_{2}}|_{\nu}^{-1}\} \displaystyle\leq\sum_{\nu\in M_{K}}N_{\nu}\,\log\max\{|a_{i}|_{\nu}\}+\sum_{\nu\in M_{K}}N_{\nu}\,\log\max\{|b_{i}|_{\nu}\}+\sum_{\nu\in M_{K}}N_{\nu}\,\log\max\{|b_{d_{2}}|_{\nu}^{-1}\} \displaystyle=h(f)+h(g)+h(b_{d_{2}}^{-1}) \displaystyle=h(f)+h(g)+h(b_{d_{2}})\leq h(f)+2h(g). $$

On the other hand, by definition, $h(f)\leq h(f,g)$ and $h(g)\leq h(f,g).$ Therefore,

$$ h(f)+2h(g)\leq 3h(f,g), $$

which proves the first assertion.

The second and third assertions then follow immediately from [61, Proposition 5] together with the first assertion. ∎

#### 6.2.2. Proof of the lower bounds for global energy pairing

Fix two integers $d_{1},d_{2}\geq 2$ . Let $f$ and $g$ be two polynomials of degree $d_{1}$ and $d_{2}$ respectively over $K$ , $f(z)=\sum_{i=0}^{d}a_{i}z^{i},$ and $g(z)=\sum_{i=0}^{d}b_{i}z^{i}.$ For any place $\nu$ of $K$ , the polynomials $f$ and $g$ can be viewed as polynomials over $\mathbb{C}_{\nu}$ .

For all but finitely many places $\nu$ , one has $\lvert\operatorname{Res}(f)\rvert_{\nu}=\lvert\operatorname{Res}(g)\rvert_{\nu}=1,$ so that both $f_{\nu}$ and $g_{\nu}$ have good reduction at $\nu$ . In this case, their associated equilibrium measures coincide, and consequently the local energy pairing $\langle f,g\rangle_{\nu}$ introduced in §2.3.3 vanishes.

This allows us to define a global energy pairing by summing the local contributions:

$$ \langle f,g\rangle:=\sum_{\nu\in M_{K}}N_{\nu}\langle f,g\rangle_{\nu}. $$

As before, the definition does not depend on the choice of the number field $K$ . We are now ready to prove the first uniform lower bound on our global energy pairing.

#### Theorem 6.3.

Let $d_{1},d_{2}\geq 2$ be fixed integers. Then there exist constants $A=A(d_{1},d_{2})>0$ and $B=B(d_{1},d_{2})>0$ such that, for every pair $(f,g)\in\mathrm{Poly}_{\mathrm{mc}}^{d_{1}}\times\mathrm{Poly}^{d_{2}}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}),$ if

$$ f^{n_{1}}\neq\lambda\,g^{n_{2}}\quad\text{for all }\lambda\in\Sigma_{f}\text{ and all }n_{1},n_{2}\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}, $$

then

$$ \langle f,g\rangle\geq A\,h(f,g)-B. $$

#### Proof of Theorem 6.3.

If $f$ is monomial, the result follows from [87, Corollary 1.4].

Let $V_{m}\subset\mathrm{Poly}_{\mathrm{mc}}^{d_{1}}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$ denote the locus of polynomials whose group of dynamical symmetries is equal to $\mathbb{U}_{m}$ . Note that

$$ \mathrm{Poly}_{\mathrm{mc}}^{d_{1}}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})\setminus\{z^{d_{1}}\}=\bigsqcup_{m=1}^{d_{1}}\left(V_{m}\setminus\bigcup_{i=2}^{d_{1}}V_{im}\right). $$

It therefore suffices to treat the case where $f\in V\setminus V^{\prime}$ , with $V=V_{m}$ and $V^{\prime}=\bigcup_{i=2}^{d_{1}}V_{im}.$ By construction, for any $f\in V\setminus V^{\prime}$ , we have $\Sigma_{f}=\mathbb{U}_{m}$ .

Recall that $V^{\prime}$ is defined by a finite collection of monic monomials $p_{1},\ldots,p_{\ell}$ . Write $f(z)=\sum_{n=0}^{d_{1}}a_{n}z^{n}$ and $g(z)=\sum_{n=0}^{d_{2}}b_{n}z^{n}$ . Let $K$ be the number field generated by $a_{i}$ and $b_{j}$ for all $0\leq i\leq d_{1}$ and $0\leq j\leq d_{2}$ . For any $\nu\in M_{K}$ , we define

$$ \lambda_{V^{\prime},\nu}(f)=-\log\max\{|p_{1}(f)|_{\nu},\ldots,|p_{\ell}(f)|_{\nu}\}. $$

Set $M:=\max_{1\leq i\leq\ell}\deg p_{i}.$

We divide the proof into the following steps.

Step 1. Suppose there exist positive integers $n_{1},n_{2}$ such that $D=d_{1}^{n_{1}}=d_{2}^{n_{2}}.$ Let $R$ be the constant appearing in Lemma 6.2. Let $R_{1}=2R+\log 2.$

We say a place $\nu\in M_{K}$ is good if the following statements hold:

- (1) $\lambda_{V^{\prime},\nu}(f)\leq 4mR_{1}(D+1)M\log|(f,g)|_{\nu}$ ;

- (2) $\min_{\lambda\in\mathbb{U}_{m}}\log|f^{n_{1}}-\lambda g^{n_{2}}|_{\nu}\geq-4mR_{1}(D+1)\log|(f,g)|_{\nu}$ .

We prove that

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{\nu\text{~good}}N_{\nu}\log|(f,g)|_{\nu}\geq\frac{1}{2}h(f,g)-\frac{1}{2}. $$

Otherwise, since $\sum_{\nu\in M_{K}}N_{\nu}\log|(f,g)|_{\nu}=h(f,g)$ , we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{\nu\text{~bad}}N_{\nu}\log|(f,g)|_{\nu}\geq\frac{1}{2}h(f,g)+\frac{1}{2}. $$

Write $f^{n_{1}}(z)=\sum_{n=0}^{D}a_{n}^{(D)}z^{n}$ and $g^{n_{2}}(z)=\sum_{n=0}^{D}b_{n}^{(D)}z^{n}$ . Let $\nu$ be a bad place. Then either (1) or (2) does not hold. Suppose (1) does not hold. Note that there exists $p_{i}$ , such that

$$ \lambda_{V^{\prime},\nu}(f)=-\log|p_{i}(f)|_{\nu}\leq M\max_{a_{i}\not=0}\log^{+}\{|a_{i}|^{-1}_{\nu}\}. $$

Therefore,

$$ 4mR_{1}(D+1)\log|(f,g)|_{\nu}<\max_{a_{i}\not=0}\log^{+}\{|a_{i}|_{\nu}^{-1}\}. $$

If (2) does not hold, then

$$ 4mR_{1}(D+1)\log|(f,g)|_{\nu}<\max_{\lambda\in\mathbb{U}_{m}}\log\min_{0\leq i\leq D}\{|a_{i}^{(D)}-\lambda b_{i}^{(D)}|^{-1}\}. $$

Using (6.5) and summing up over all bad places, one obtains

$$ \displaystyle 2m(D+1)(R_{1}h(f,g)+R_{1}) \displaystyle\leq\sum_{\nu~\text{bad}}N_{\nu}\max_{\lambda\in\mathbb{U}_{m},~a_{j}\not=0}\max\{\log^{+}\min_{0\leq i\leq D}\{|a_{i}^{(D)}-\lambda b_{i}^{(D)}|_{\nu}^{-1}\},\log^{+}\{|a_{j}|_{\nu}^{-1}\}\} \displaystyle<\sum_{\nu\in\mathrm{M}_{K}}N_{\nu}\max_{\lambda\in\mathbb{U}_{m},~a_{j}\not=0}\max\{\log^{+}\min_{0\leq i\leq D}\{|a_{i}^{(D)}-\lambda b_{i}^{(D)}|_{\nu}^{-1}\},\log^{+}\{|a_{j}|_{\nu}^{-1}\}\}, $$

which is at most

$$ \left(\sum_{\lambda\in\mathbb{U}_{m},a_{j}\not=0}\sum_{\nu\in M_{K}}N_{\nu}\log^{+}\min_{0\leq i\leq D}\{|a_{i}^{(D)}-\lambda b_{i}^{(D)}|_{\nu}^{-1}\}\right)+\left(\sum_{a_{j}\not=0}mN_{\nu}\log^{+}\{|a_{j}|_{\nu}^{-1}\}\right). $$

By the pigeonhole principle, either there exist $\lambda\in\mathbb{U}_{m},$ $a_{i}^{(D)}\not=\lambda b_{i}^{(D)}$ such that

$$ R_{1}h(f,g)+R_{1}<\sum_{\nu\in\mathrm{M}_{K}}N_{\nu}\log^{+}\{|a_{i}^{(D)}-\lambda b_{i}^{(D)}|_{\nu}^{-1}\}=h(a_{i}^{(D)}-\lambda b_{i}^{(D)}) $$

or there exists $a_{i}\not=0$ , such that

$$ R_{1}h(f,g)+R_{1}<\sum_{\nu\in\mathrm{M}_{K}}N_{\nu}\log^{+}\{|a_{i}|_{\nu}^{-1}\}=h(a_{i}). $$

By Lemma 6.2, we have $R_{1}h(f,g)+R_{1}\geq h(a_{i})$ and

$$ h(a_{i}^{(D)}-\lambda b_{i}^{(D)})\leq h(a_{i}^{(D)})+h(b_{i}^{(D)})+\log 2\leq 2h(f^{n_{1}},g^{n_{2}})+\log 2\leq R_{1}h(f,g)+R_{1}. $$

This yields a contradiction.

Step 2. Suppose there do not exist positive integers $n_{1}$ and $n_{2}$ such that $d_{1}^{n_{1}}=d_{2}^{n_{2}}$ .

We say a place $\nu\in M_{K}$ is good if $\lambda_{V^{\prime},\nu}(f)\leq 2(d+1)M\log|(f,g)|_{\nu},$ where $d=\max\{d_{1},d_{2}\}$ .

We prove that

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{\nu\text{~good}}N_{\nu}\log|(f,g)|_{\nu}\geq\frac{1}{2}h(f,g)-\frac{1}{2}. $$

Otherwise, since $\sum_{\nu\in M_{K}}N_{\nu}\log|(f,g)|_{\nu}=h(f,g)$ , we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{\nu\text{~bad}}N_{\nu}\log|(f,g)|_{\nu}\geq\frac{1}{2}h(f,g)+\frac{1}{2}. $$

Let $\nu$ be a bad place. Note that there exists $p_{i}$ , such that

$$ \lambda_{V^{\prime},\nu}(f)=-\log|p_{i}(f)|_{\nu}\leq M\max_{a_{i}\not=0}\log^{+}\{|a_{i}|^{-1}_{\nu}\}. $$

Therefore,

$$ 2(d+1)\log|(f,g)|_{\nu}<\max_{a_{i}\not=0}\log^{+}\{|a_{i}|_{\nu}^{-1}\}. $$

Using (6.7) and summing up over all bad places, one obtains

$$ \displaystyle(d+1)(h(f,g)+1) \displaystyle\leq\sum_{\nu~\text{bad}}N_{\nu}\max_{a_{i}\not=0}\{\log^{+}\{|a_{i}|_{\nu}^{-1}\}\} $$

By the pigeonhole principle, there exists $a_{i}\not=0$ , such that

$$ h(f,g)+1<\sum_{\nu\in\mathrm{M}_{K}}N_{\nu}\log^{+}\{|a_{i}|_{\nu}^{-1}\}=h(a_{i}). $$

Since $h(f,g)\geq h(a_{i})$ , we obtain a contradiction.

Step 3. Conclusion. If there exist positive integers $n_{1},n_{2}$ such that $D=d_{1}^{n_{1}}=d_{2}^{n_{2}}$ . Let $C_{1}=4mR_{1}(D+1)M$ and $C_{2}=4mR_{1}(D+1)$ , otherwise take $C_{1}=2(\max\{d_{1},d_{2}\}+1)M$ . Let $C_{5}$ be the constant appearing in Theorem 1.7. For any good place $\nu$ , we distinguish two cases according to whether the residue characteristic of $\mathbb{C}_{\nu}$ is $<C_{5}$ or $\geq C_{5}$ .

In the former case, since $\mathbb{C}_{\nu}$ has finitely many choices up to isometry, by Theorem 1.6, there exist uniform constants $A_{1},B_{1}>0$ , such that

$$ \langle f,g\rangle_{\nu}\geq A_{1}\log|(f,g)|_{\nu}-B_{1}. $$

Note that for any prime number $p$ , one has $\sum_{\nu\mid p}N_{\nu}=1.$ Therefore,

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\nu\ \text{good}\\
\mathrm{char}(\tilde{\mathbb{C}}_{\nu})<C_{5}\end{subarray}}N_{\nu}\langle f,g\rangle_{\nu}\geq-B_{1}C_{5}+A_{1}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\nu\ \text{good}\\
\mathrm{char}(\tilde{\mathbb{C}}_{\nu})<C_{5}\end{subarray}}N_{\nu}\log|(f,g)|_{\nu}. $$

In the latter case, by Theorem 1.7, there exist uniform constants $A_{2}>0$ , such that

$$ \langle f,g\rangle_{\nu}\geq A_{2}\log|(f,g)|_{\nu}. $$

Therefore,

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\nu\ \text{good}\\
\mathrm{char}(\tilde{\mathbb{C}}_{\nu})\geq C_{5}\end{subarray}}N_{\nu}\langle f,g\rangle_{\nu}\geq A_{2}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\nu\ \text{good}\\
\mathrm{char}(\tilde{\mathbb{C}}_{\nu})\geq C_{5}\end{subarray}}N_{\nu}\log|(f,g)|_{\nu}. $$

Let $A=\tfrac{1}{2}\min\{A_{1},A_{2}\}$ and $B=B_{1}C_{5}+\tfrac{A}{2}$ . Summing (6.8) and (6.9), and using (6.4) and (6.6), we obtain

$$ \langle f,g\rangle\geq\sum_{\nu\ \mathrm{good}}N_{\nu}\langle f,g\rangle_{\nu}\geq A\,h(f,g)-B. $$

This completes the proof. ∎

We now prove the second uniform lower bound on our global energy pairing.

#### Theorem 6.4.

Let $d_{1},d_{2}\geq 2$ be fixed integers. Then there exists a constant $\delta=\delta(d_{1},d_{2})>0$ , such that for any two polynomials $(f,g)\in\mathrm{Poly}_{\mathrm{mc}}^{d_{1}}\times\mathrm{Poly}^{d_{2}}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$ satisfying

$$ f^{n_{1}}\neq\lambda\,g^{n_{2}}\quad\text{for all }\lambda\in\Sigma_{f}\text{ and all }n_{1},n_{2}\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}, $$

we have

$$ \langle f,g\rangle\geq\delta. $$

#### Proof.

The case where $f$ is monomial and $g$ is monic follows from [83, Proposition 5.6]. The proof easily extends to the non-monic case as $g$ is assumed to have a non-zero coefficient that is not the leading coefficient.

We may then suppose that $f$ is not monomial. Let $V_{m}$ denote the set of polynomials whose group of dynamical symmetries is equal to $\mathbb{U}_{m}$ . Since $\mathrm{Poly}_{\mathrm{mc}}^{d_{1}}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})\setminus\{z^{d_{1}}\}=\bigsqcup_{m=1}^{d_{1}}\left(V_{m}\setminus\bigcup_{i=2}^{d_{1}}V_{im}\right),$ it suffices to consider the case where $f\in V\setminus V^{\prime}$ , with $V=V_{m}$ and $V^{\prime}=\bigcup_{i=2}^{d}V_{im}.$ By construction, any $f\in V\setminus V^{\prime}$ satisfies $\Sigma_{f}=\mathbb{U}_{m}$ .

If there exist positive integers $n_{1},n_{2}$ such that $d_{1}^{n_{1}}=d_{2}^{n_{2}}$ , up to iteration, we may suppose $d_{1}=d_{2}=d.$

By Theorem 6.3, if $h(f,g)$ is sufficiently large, then the conclusion follows. Hence, we may assume that there exists a constant $C>1$ such that $h(f,g)<C.$

Let $|\cdot|_{\infty}$ denote the standard Euclidean norm on $\mathbb{C}$ . We consider pairs $(f,g)$ satisfying the following four conditions:

- (1) $\log|f|_{\infty}\leq 8C$ ;

- (2) $\log|g|_{\infty}\leq 8C$ ;

- (3) $-\log\max_{1\leq i\leq m}|p_{i}(f)|_{\infty}\leq 8CM$ .

When $d_{1}=d_{2}=d$ , we further suppose

- (4) $\min_{\lambda\in\mathbb{U}_{m}}\log|f-\lambda g|_{\nu}\geq-8m(d+1)(2C+\log 2)$ .

These conditions define a compact subset $Y\subset(V\setminus V^{\prime})\times\mathrm{Poly}^{d_{2}}(\mathbb{C})\setminus E,$ where $E=\emptyset$ if $d_{1}\not=d_{2}$ and $E=\{((V\setminus V^{\prime})\times\mathrm{Poly}^{d_{2}}(\mathbb{C}):f=\lambda g\text{ for some }\lambda\in\mathbb{U}_{m}\}$ if $d_{1}=d_{2}.$

By the complex rigidity of Julia sets [93], for $(f,g)\in X$ we have $\langle f,g\rangle_{\infty}=0$ if and only if $(f,g)\in E$ . Therefore, by continuity of the local energy pairing and compactness of $Y$ , there exists a constant $\delta>0$ such that $\langle f,g\rangle_{\infty}\geq 2\delta$ for all $(f,g)\in Y.$

Now choose a number field $K$ containing the coefficients of both $f$ and $g$ . Denote by $\sigma_{\nu}:K\hookrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ the embedding corresponding to an Archimedean place $v\mid\infty$ .

We say that an Archimedean place $\nu$ is good if $(\sigma_{\nu}(f),\sigma_{\nu}(g))\in Y.$ We claim that if $h(f,g)<C$ , then $\sum_{\nu\ \mathrm{good}}N_{\nu}\geq\frac{1}{2}.$

Assuming the claim, we obtain

$$ \langle f,g\rangle\geq\sum_{\nu\mid\infty}N_{\nu}\langle f,g\rangle_{\nu}\geq\sum_{\nu\ \mathrm{good}}N_{\nu}\langle f,g\rangle_{\nu}\geq\sum_{\nu\ \mathrm{good}}2N_{\nu}\delta\geq\delta, $$

which completes the proof.

It remains to prove the claim. Since $\sum_{\nu\mid\infty}N_{\nu}=1$ , if the claim were false, we would have $\sum_{\nu\ \mathrm{bad}}N_{\nu}>\frac{1}{2}.$ Each bad place $\nu$ must violate at least one of the defining conditions of $Y$ , that is, at least one of the following holds:

- (1) $\log|f|_{\nu}>8C$ ,

- (2) $\log|g|_{\nu}>8C$ ,

- (3) $-\log\max_{1\leq i\leq l}|p_{i}(f)|_{\nu}>8CM$ .

When $d_{1}=d_{2}=d$ , we further suppose

- (4) $\min_{\lambda\in\mathbb{U}_{m}}\log|f-\lambda g|_{\nu}<-8m(d+1)(2C+\log 2)$ .

By the pigeonhole principle, for at least one of these four cases the total sum of the corresponding $N_{\nu}$ is at least $1/8$ .

If this occurs in case (1), then

$$ h(f,g)\geq\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\nu\mid\infty\\
|f|_{\nu}>8C\end{subarray}}N_{\nu}\log|f|_{\nu}>C, $$

contradicting $h(f,g)<C$ . Case (2) is identical.

In case (3), write $f(z)=\sum_{n=0}^{d_{1}}a_{n}z^{n}$ and $g(z)=\sum_{n=0}^{d_{2}}b_{n}z^{n}.$ Then there exists $i$ such that $a_{i}\not=0$ while $\log^{+}|a_{i}^{-1}|_{\nu}\geq 8C.$ Hence

$$ h(f,g)\geq h(a_{i})\geq\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\nu\mid\infty\\
\text{(3) holds}\end{subarray}}N_{\nu}\log^{+}|a_{i}^{-1}|_{\nu}\geq C, $$

a contradiction.

Finally, suppose case (4) occurs. Then there exists $i$ and $\lambda\in\mathbb{U}_{m}$ such that $a_{i}\neq\lambda b_{i}$ and $\log|a_{i}-\lambda b_{i}|_{\nu}<-8(2C+\log 2).$ Thus

$$ h(a_{i}-\lambda b_{i})=h((a_{i}-\lambda b_{i})^{-1})\geq\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\nu\mid\infty\\
\text{(4) holds}\end{subarray}}N_{\nu}\log(|a_{i}-\lambda b_{i}|_{\nu}^{-1})>2C+\log 2. $$

By Lemma 6.2, one has

$$ C>h(f,g)\geq\frac{1}{2}\bigl(h(a_{i})+h(b_{i})\bigr)\geq\frac{1}{2}\bigl(h(a_{i}-\lambda b_{i})-\log 2\bigr)>C, $$

again a contradiction.

Therefore all cases lead to contradictions, and the claim follows. ∎

### 6.3. Proof of Theorem 1.2

We may now combine Theorems 6.3 and 6.4 to prove Theorem 1.2. By a specialization argument [30, §10.2], we may assume that $f,g\in\overline{\mathbb{Q}}[z]$ . By conjugating both $f$ and $g$ by an affine transformation, we may further assume that $f$ is monic centered.

Suppose there exist $\lambda\in\Sigma_{f}$ and positive integers $n_{1},n_{2}$ such that $f^{n_{1}}=\lambda g^{n_{2}}$ . Let $D=d_{1}^{n_{1}}=d_{2}^{n_{2}}$ . By induction, for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$ , the iterations of $f$ and $g$ satisfy

$$ f^{n_{1}n}(z)=\lambda^{1+D+\cdots+D^{\,n-1}}g^{n_{2}n}(z). $$

Since $\lambda$ is a root of unity, it follows that $z$ has finite orbit under $f$ if and only if it has finite orbit under $g$ . Therefore, $\operatorname{Prep}(f)=\operatorname{Prep}(g).$

Now suppose otherwise. By [57, Theorem B], if $N=\bigl|\operatorname{Prep}(f)\cap\operatorname{Prep}(g)\bigr|\geq 2,$ then there exists a constant $C=C(d_{1},d_{2})>0$ such that

$$ \langle f,g\rangle\leq C\left(\frac{1}{N}+\frac{\log N}{N}\right)\bigl(h(f,g)+1\bigr)\leq 2C\frac{\log N}{N}(h(f,g)+1). $$

On the other hand, by Theorems 6.3 and 6.4, there exist uniform constants $A,B,\delta>0$ , depending only on the degrees, such that $\langle f,g\rangle\geq\delta$ and $\langle f,g\rangle\geq A\,h(f,g)-B.$

Suppose $h(f,g)\geq\frac{2(B+2C)}{A}.$ We claim that

$$ \frac{\log N}{N}\geq\frac{A}{4C}, $$

hence $N$ is uniformly bounded. If the claim does not hold, applying (6.10), we have

$$ B+2C<\left(A-2C\frac{\log N}{N}\right)h(f,g)\leq B+2C, $$

which leads to a contradiction.

Suppose $h(f,g)<\frac{2(B+2C)}{A}.$ Applying (6.10) again, we obtain

$$ \frac{\log N}{N}\geq\frac{\delta A}{2C(2B+4C+A)}. $$

Thus $N$ is uniformly bounded, which completes the proof.

## 7. DeMarco–Mavraki Conjecture for Fibered Powers of $\Delta$

### 7.1. DeMarco–Mavraki conjecture

We now prove the following special case of the relative Dynamical Bogomolov conjecture. Let $X\subseteq\mathrm{Poly}_{\mathrm{mc}}^{d_{1}}\times\mathrm{Poly}^{d_{2}}$ be a closed irreducible subvariety of dimension $k$ defined over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ . Let $\Delta\subseteq(\mathbb{P}^{1})^{2}$ be the diagonal and consider the fibered power $\Delta^{k+1}\times X\subseteq(\mathbb{P}^{1})^{2(k+1)}\times\mathrm{Poly}_{\mathrm{mc}}^{d}\times\mathrm{Poly}^{d}$ . For a point $x=(x_{1},x_{2})\in\mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb{C})\times\mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb{C})$ , we will let $\widehat{h}_{f,g}(x)=\widehat{h}_{f}(x_{1})+\widehat{h}_{g}(x_{2}).$

#### Theorem 7.1.

Assume that as $(f,g)$ varies over $X(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$ , the map $f$ is not always $z^{d_{1}}$ . Further assume that $\operatorname{Prep}(f)\not=\operatorname{Prep}(g)$ for some $(f,g)\in X$ . Then there exists $\varepsilon>0$ the set

$$ \left\{(x_{1},\ldots,x_{k+1},f,g)\text{ }\bigg|\text{ }\sum_{i=1}^{k+1}\widehat{h}_{f,g}(x_{i})<\varepsilon\right\}\subset(\Delta)^{k+1}\times X $$

is not Zariski dense in $(\Delta)^{k+1}\times X$ .

We have to exclude the case where $f$ is always a monomial map as there are counterexamples. For example, consider the family $(z^{d},cz^{d})$ as $c$ varies in $\mathbb{A}^{1}$ . Then if $c$ is a root of unity, we have $\operatorname{Prep}(z^{d})=\operatorname{Prep}(cz^{d})$ which gives us a Zariski dense set of bad parameters in $\mathbb{A}^{1}$ .

Theorem 7.1 can be viewed as a special case to the DeMarco–Mavraki conjecture [33, Conjecture 1.1], which we will recall the statement now. Let $S$ be a smooth and irreducible quasi-projective variety over $\mathbb{C}$ and let $\Phi:S\times\mathbb{P}^{N}\to S\times\mathbb{P}^{N}$ be an algebraic family of endomorphisms of degree $d$ , i.e. $\Phi(s,x)=\Phi(s,f_{s}(x))$ where $f_{s}:\mathbb{P}^{n}\to\mathbb{P}^{N}$ is an endomorphism of degree $d$ . The smoothness of $S$ is not important as one can always apply resolution of singularities to the base to obtain a smooth family. We will denote the function field of $S$ by $\mathbb{C}(S)$ . Let $\cal{X}\subseteq S\times\mathbb{P}^{N}$ be a closed irreducible subvariety flat over $S$ . Given an irreducible subvariety $\cal{Y}\subset S\times\mathbb{P}^{N}$ which is flat over a Zariski open, we say $\cal{Y}$ is $\Phi$ -special if there exists a subvariety $\mathbf{Z}\subseteq\mathbb{P}^{N}_{\overline{\mathbb{C}(S)}}$ containing the generic fiber $\mathbf{Y}$ of $\cal{Y}$ and a polarizable endomorphism $\mathbf{\Psi}:\mathbf{Z}\to\mathbf{Z}$ over $\overline{\mathbb{C}(S)}$ such that for some $n\in\mathbb{N}$ , the following hold:

- (1) $\mathbf{\Psi}^{n}(\mathbf{Z})=\mathbf{Z}$ ;

- (2) $\mathbf{\Psi}^{n}\circ\mathbf{\Phi}=\mathbf{\Phi}\circ\mathbf{\Psi}^{n}$ on $\mathbf{Z}$ where $\mathbf{\Phi}$ is the generic fiber of $\Phi$ ;

- (3) $\mathbf{Y}$ is preperiodic for $\Psi$ .

We will let $r_{\Phi,\cal{X}}$ denote the relative special dimension of $\cal{X}$ over $S$ , i.e.

$$ r_{\Phi,\cal{X}}:=\min\{\dim\cal{Y}-\dim S\mid\cal{Y}\text{ is }\Phi-\text{special}\text{ and }\cal{X}\subset\cal{Y}\}. $$

Now let $\widehat{T}_{\Phi}$ denote the dynamical $(1,1)$ -Green current associated to $\Phi$ [55]. We can now state the DeMarco–Mavraki conjecture.

#### Conjecture 7.2.

The following are equivalent:

- (1) $\cal{X}$ contains a Zariski dense set of $\Phi$ -preperiodic points;

- (2) $\widehat{T}_{\Phi}^{\wedge r_{\Phi,\cal{X}}}\wedge[\cal{X}]\not=0.$

The implication $(2\Rightarrow(1)$ is [33, Theorem 1.5]. Hence the difficulty of the conjecture is to show that if $\widehat{T}_{\Phi}^{\wedge r_{\Phi,\cal{X}}}\wedge[\cal{X}]=0$ , then $\cal{X}$ does not contain a Zariski dense set of preperiodic points.

The DeMarco–Mavraki conjecture can be viewed as a dynamical generalization of the Relative Manin–Mumford conjecture, proven by Gao and Habegger [54]. The reader may consult [33] for some striking consequences of the conjecture. The relative Bogomolov conjecture was also proven for fibered powers of elliptic curves by Kühne [74].

Combining Theorem 7.1 and implication $(2)\Rightarrow(1)$ for Conjecture 7.2, we obtain that the DeMarco–Mavraki conjecture is true for $\cal{X}=(\Delta)^{k}\times X$ for any $k$ . We restrict ourselves to the case of equal degrees as the DeMarco–Mavraki conjecture is originally stated only for polarized dynamical systems.

#### Theorem 7.3.

Let $X\subseteq\mathrm{Poly}_{\mathrm{mc}}^{d}\times\mathrm{Poly}^{d}$ be an irreducible subvariety defined over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ . Assume that as $(f,g)$ varies over $X(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$ , the map $f$ is not always $z^{d}$ . Fix a positive integer $k$ and let

$$ \cal{X}=(\Delta)^{k}\times X\subseteq(\mathbb{P}^{1})^{2k}\times X, $$

where we view $\cal{X}$ as a family over the base $X$ . Then the DeMarco–Mavraki conjecture is true for $\cal{X}$ .

As remarked previously, Theorem 7.1 can be viewed as a relative version of the Dynamical Manin–Mumford. It is easy to deduce a uniform bound on $|\operatorname{Prep}(f)\cap\operatorname{Prep}(g)|$ over a Zariski open $U$ of $X$ from Theorem 7.1. Conversely, if one knew the existence of a Zariski open $U$ and $N=N(d)>0$ such that $|\operatorname{Prep}(f)\cap\operatorname{Prep}(g)|\leq N$ for all $(f,g)\in U$ , then the set

$$ \{(x_{1},\ldots,x_{N+1},f,g)\mid x_{i}\in\operatorname{Prep}(f)\cap\operatorname{Prep}(g)\}\subset(\Delta)^{N+1}\times U $$

is contained in the union of $\{x_{i}=x_{j}\}$ over all pairs $(i,j)$ . The extra content of Theorem 7.1 is that we only have to pass to a $(\dim X+1)$ -fibered power to have the special points lie in a Zariski closed subset.

We will deduce Theorem 7.1 by combining [105, Theorem 4.1] with our uniform lower bounds in a similar fashion that Yuan deduces his uniform Bogomolov-type statements. We now recall the theory of adelic line bundles over quasi-projective varieties.

### 7.2. Adelic line bundles over quasi-projective varieties

We will be using the theory of adelic line bundles over quasi-projective varieties which the reader may refer to [103] for the details. We first briefly review the basic definitions. Let $X$ be a flat integral projective scheme over $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb{Z}$ . Then an arithmetic $\mathbb{Q}$ -divisor $\cal{D}$ is a pair $(D,g_{\cal{D}})$ where $D$ is a $\mathbb{Q}$ -Cartier divisor and $g_{\cal{D}}$ a continuous Green’s function for the divisor $D$ on $X(\mathbb{C})$ . Now if $U$ is a quasi-projective scheme flat over $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb{Z}$ , we define the space of arithemtic model divisors $\widehat{\operatorname{Div}}_{\mathbb{Q}}(U)_{\mathrm{mod}}$ as

$$ \widehat{\operatorname{Div}}_{\mathbb{Q}}(U)_{\mathrm{mod}}=\lim_{\rightarrow}\widehat{\operatorname{Div}}_{\mathbb{Q}}(X) $$

where $X$ ranges over all compactifications of $U$ . Fixing some compactification $\overline{U}$ , we may define a boundary divisor $\cal{E}$ which is a model divisor whose suppport is $\overline{U}\setminus U$ and whose Green’s function satisfies $g_{\cal{E}}>0$ everywhere. We may then endow $\widehat{\operatorname{Div}}_{\mathbb{Q}}(U)_{\mathrm{mod}}$ with a suitable boundary topology and form its completion, giving us the space $\widehat{\operatorname{Div}}_{\mathbb{Q}}(U)$ . Quotienting out by a suitable equivalence gives us the space of adelic line bundles $\widehat{\operatorname{Pic}}(U/\mathbb{Z})$ .

Finally if $X$ is simply a quasi-projective variety over a number field $K$ , we will let

$$ \widehat{\operatorname{Pic}}(X/\mathbb{Z}):=\lim_{\rightarrow}\widehat{\operatorname{Pic}}(\cal{U}/\mathbb{Z}) $$

where the limit is taken over all quasi-projective models $\cal{U}$ of $X$ over $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb{Z}$ .

The space $\widehat{\operatorname{Pic}}(X/\mathbb{Z})$ is usually too big and we will work with a subset of it known as the integrable adelic line bundles for which a good notion of intersection theory can be developed. We will denote the set of integrable adelic line bundles by $\widehat{\operatorname{Pic}}(X/\mathbb{Z})_{\operatorname{int}}$ .

We now start recalling some basic results that we will now need. Given an integral scheme $S$ , we say $(X,f,L)$ is a polarized dynamical system over $S$ if the following holds:

- (1) $X$ is an integral projective scheme over $S$ ;

- (2) $f:X\to X$ is a morphism over $S$ ;

- (3) $L$ is a $\mathbb{Q}$ -line bundle on $X$ , relatively ample over $S$ and there exists $q>1$ such that $f^{*}L\simeq qL$ .

#### Proposition 7.4.

Let $S$ be a quasi-projective variety over a number field $K$ with an affine quasi-projective model over $\mathbb{Z}$ . Let $(X,f,L)$ be a polarized dynamical system over $S$ . Then there exists an integrable nef adelic line bundle $\overline{L}_{f}\in\widehat{\operatorname{Pic}}(X/\mathbb{Z})$ such that $f^{*}\overline{L}_{f}=q\overline{L}_{f}$ .

#### Proof.

This is [103, Theorem 6.1.1]. ∎

We now recall the Deligne pairing for adelic line bundles over quasi-projective varieties. Again let $K$ be a number field and let $Y$ be a normal quasi-projective variety over $K$ . Let $f:X\to Y$ be a projective and flat morphism of relative dimension $n$ and assume that $X$ is integral. Then the Deligne pairing [103, Theorem 4.1.3] induces a symmetric and multilinear functor

$$ \widehat{\operatorname{Pic}}(X/\mathbb{Z})_{\operatorname{int}}^{n+1}\to\widehat{\operatorname{Pic}}(Y/\mathbb{Z})_{\operatorname{int}}. $$

We denote the image of $(\overline{L}_{1},\ldots,\overline{L}_{n+1})$ by $f_{*}\langle\overline{L}_{1},\ldots,\overline{L}_{n+1}\rangle$ . Furthermore, the Deligne pairing functor is compatible by base change, giving us the following interpretation of heights under the Deligne pairing.

#### Proposition 7.5.

Let $\overline{L}_{1},\ldots,\overline{L}_{n+1}$ be $n+1$ integrable adelic line bundles on $X$ and let $\overline{M}=\langle\overline{L}_{1},\ldots,\overline{L}_{n+1}\rangle\in\widehat{\operatorname{Pic}}(Y/\mathbb{Z})_{\operatorname{int}}$ . Let $s\in Y(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$ . Then

$$ h_{\overline{M}}(s)=h_{\overline{L}_{1},\ldots,\overline{L}_{n+1}}(X_{s}). $$

#### Proof.

This follows from functoriality of the Deligne pairing by base change, see the proof of [103, Lemma 6.3.2]. ∎

We next recall the definition of a big line bundle. For any adelic line bundle $\overline{L}$ , we may define an arithmetic volume function $\widehat{\operatorname{vol}}(\overline{L})$ [103, Section 5.2]. We say that $\overline{L}$ is big if $\widehat{\operatorname{vol}}(\overline{L})>0$ . The bigness of $\overline{L}$ directly implies the non-Zariski density of small points for $h_{\overline{L}}$ , as seen in [103, Theorem 5.3.7]. We will need a weaker condition called potential bigness. Again for our morphism $f:X\to Y$ of pure relative dimension $n$ , we say that an adelic line bundle $\overline{L}$ on $X$ is potentially big if the adelic line bundle

$$ \overline{L}^{\boxtimes m}=(p_{1}^{*}\overline{L})\otimes\cdots\otimes(p_{m}^{*}\overline{L}) $$

is big on the $m$ -fold fiber product

$$ X_{/Y}^{m}=X\times_{Y}\cdots\times_{Y}X $$

for all $m\geq\dim Y+1$ . The following proposition of Yuan gives a criterion for potential bigness in terms of the bigness of the Deligne pairing.

#### Proposition 7.6.

Assume that the generic fiber of $f:X\to Y$ is geometrically integral. Let $\overline{L}$ be an adelic line bundle on $X$ which is nef, and that the degree of $L$ on the fibers $X\to Y$ is strictly positive. Then $\overline{L}$ is potentially big if and only if the Deligne pairing $f_{*}(\overline{L},\ldots,\overline{L})$ is big,

#### Proof.

This is [105, Theorem 4.1]. Note that we have to take $m\geq\dim Y+1$ as the dimension in Yuan’s theorem is the dimension over $\mathbb{Z}$ and thus we have to add one to it. ∎

Finally we have a criterion for bigness of a line bundle $\overline{L}$ on $X$ .

#### Proposition 7.7.

Let $\overline{L}$ and $\overline{M}$ be adelic line bundle on $X$ and assume that $\overline{L}$ is nef and $\overline{M}$ is big. Then if there exists a Zariski open $U\subseteq X$ and constants $\varepsilon>0$ such that

$$ h_{\overline{L}}(x)\geq\varepsilon h_{\overline{M}}(x)\text{ for all }x\in U(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}), $$

then $\overline{L}$ is also big.

#### Proof.

We combine a few results in [103, Section 5]. First by [103, Theorem 5.3.8], if $\tilde{L}$ denotes the image of $\overline{L}$ in $\widehat{\operatorname{Pic}}(X/K)$ , then $\tilde{L}$ is big. By [103, Lemma 5.3.4], as $\widehat{\operatorname{vol}}(\overline{M})>0$ , it follows that its first essential minimum $e_{1}(X,\overline{M})>0$ . Then our inequality implies that $e_{1}(X,\overline{L})>0$ too. By [103, Theorem 5.3.3], as we know that $\tilde{L}$ is big, it follows that $h_{\overline{L}}(X)>0$ . By [103, Theorem 5.2.2], it follows that $\widehat{\operatorname{vol}}(\overline{L})>0$ and hence $\overline{L}$ is big as desired. ∎

### 7.3. Proofs of Theorems 7.1 and 7.3

We now begin the proofs of Theorem 7.1 and 7.3. We first begin with the setup. Consider $Y=\mathbb{P}^{1}\times\mathrm{Poly}_{\mathrm{mc}}^{d_{1}}$ as a variety over the base $\mathrm{Poly}_{\mathrm{mc}}^{d_{1}}$ which is a quasi-projective variety over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ . Then we have a natural endomorphism $f:Y\to Y$ over $S$ which is polarizable of degree $d\geq 2$ using the line bundle $L=O(1)$ . By Proposition 7.4, there exists an integrable adelic line bundle $\overline{L}_{f}\in\widehat{\operatorname{Pic}}(Y/\mathbb{Z})$ satisfying $f^{*}\overline{L}_{f}\simeq d_{1}\overline{L}_{f}$ . Similarly for $Z=\mathbb{P}^{1}\times\mathrm{Poly}^{d_{2}}$ , we obtain an adelic line bundle $\overline{L}_{g}\in\widehat{\operatorname{Pic}}(Z/\mathbb{Z})$ satisfying $g^{*}\overline{L}_{g}\simeq d_{2}\overline{L}_{g}$ .

Now on $Y\times Z=\mathbb{P}^{1}\times\mathrm{Poly}_{\mathrm{mc}}^{d_{1}}\times\mathbb{P}^{1}\times\mathrm{Poly}^{d_{2}}$ , we may consider the adelic line bundle $\overline{L}=\pi_{1}^{*}\overline{L}_{f}-\pi_{2}^{*}\overline{L}_{g}\in\widehat{\operatorname{Pic}}(Y\times Z/\mathbb{Z})$ and we restrict it to $\Delta^{\prime}=\Delta\times\mathrm{Poly}_{\mathrm{mc}}^{d_{1}}\times\mathrm{Poly}^{d_{2}}$ to obtain an adelic line bundle $\overline{L}\in\widehat{\operatorname{Pic}}(\Delta^{\prime}/\mathbb{Z})$ . Now $\Delta^{\prime}$ is a flat family of relative dimension $1$ over the base $\mathrm{Poly}_{\mathrm{mc}}^{d}\times\mathrm{Poly}^{d}$ and the base is certainly normal. We may thus consider the Deligne pairing

$$ \overline{M}=\langle\overline{L},\overline{L}\rangle\in\widehat{\operatorname{Pic}}(\mathrm{Poly}_{\mathrm{mc}}^{d_{1}}\times\mathrm{Poly}^{d_{2}}/\mathbb{Z}). $$

Now consider a subvariety $X\subset\mathrm{Poly}_{\mathrm{mc}}^{d_{1}}\times\mathrm{Poly}^{d_{2}}$ . Let $\nu:X^{\prime}\to X$ be its normalization. We aim to prove that $\overline{L}$ is potentially big on $\Delta\times X$ .

#### Proposition 7.8.

Assume that as $(f,g)$ varies over $X(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$ , the map $f$ is not always the monomial map. If not all $s\in X(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$ satisfy $\operatorname{Prep}(f_{s})=\operatorname{Prep}(g_{s})$ , then the adelic line bundle $\overline{L}$ is potentailly big on $\Delta\times X$ .

#### Proof.

We first show that the set of points $s\in X(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$ that do satisfy $\operatorname{Prep}(f_{s})=\operatorname{Prep}(g_{s})$ is contained in a proper Zariski closed subset.If $\operatorname{Prep}(f)=\operatorname{Prep}(g)$ , then for some Archimedean place $\nu$ , we must have $\mu_{f,v}=\mu_{g,v}$ . Fix some $(n_{1},n_{2})$ such that $d_{1}^{n_{1}}=d_{2}^{n_{2}}$ . If they don’t exist then the locus where $\mu_{f,v}=\mu_{g,v}$ is just empty. Otherwise, we obtain $f^{n_{1}}=\lambda g^{n_{2}}$ for some $\lambda\in\mathrm{Aut}(J(f))$ . On a Zariski open $U\subseteq X$ , we have that $\mathrm{Aut}(J(f))=\{\zeta^{m}=1\}$ for some $m\geq 1$ as $f$ is generically not the monomial map Then $\{f^{n_{1}}=\lambda g^{n_{2}}\}$ for $\lambda\in\mathrm{Aut}(J(f))$ cuts out a Zariski closed subset of $X$ which is not the whole space as desired as otherwise $\operatorname{Prep}(f_{s})=\operatorname{Prep}(g_{s})$ for all $s\in X(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$ .

Let $W$ be a Zariski closed subset containing all $s$ for which $\operatorname{Prep}(f_{s})=\operatorname{Prep}(g_{s})$ and let $U$ be its complement. Now by Theorems 6.3 and 6.4, along with Proposition 7.5, it follows that

$$ h_{\overline{M}}(s)\geq Ah(f,g)+B $$

for some constants $A,B>0$ , for all $s\in U(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$ . Since $\nu:X^{\prime}\to X$ is birational, the potential bigness of $\overline{L}$ on $X\times\Delta$ is equivalent to that of $\nu^{*}\overline{L}$ on $X^{\prime}\times\Delta$ . Using Proposition 7.6, it suffices to prove that $\nu^{*}\overline{M}$ is big, which again is equivalent to $\overline{M}$ being big. Now as the Weil height $h(f,g)$ comes from the height of a big adelic line bundle, by Proposition 7.7 it follows that $\overline{M}$ is big and hence $\overline{L}$ is potentially big on $X\times\Delta$ . ∎

#### Theorem 7.9.

Assume that as $(f,g)$ varies over $X(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$ , the map $f$ is not always $z^{d_{1}}$ . Further assume that $\operatorname{Prep}(f)\not=\operatorname{Prep}(g)$ for some $(f,g)\in X$ . Then there exists $\varepsilon>0$ the set

$$ \left\{(x_{1},\ldots,x_{k+1},f,g)\text{ }\bigg|\text{ }\sum_{i=1}^{k+1}\widehat{h}_{f,g}(x_{i})<\varepsilon\right\}\subset(\Delta)^{k+1}\times X $$

is not Zariski dense in $(\Delta)^{k+1}\times X$ .

#### Proof.

By Proposition 7.8, we know that $\overline{L}$ is potentially big on $X\times\Delta$ over $X$ . Hence if $k=\dim X$ , it follows that $\overline{L}^{\boxtimes k+1}$ is big on $\Delta^{k+1}\times X$ . The height function induced by $\overline{L}^{\boxtimes k+1}$ is equivalent to $\sum_{i=1}^{k+1}\widehat{h}_{f,g}(x_{i})$ . It thus follows there exists an $\varepsilon>0$ points of height $<\varepsilon$ is not Zariski dense in $(\Delta)^{k+1}\times X$ as desired. ∎

We now prove Theorem 7.3.

#### Theorem 7.10.

Let $X\subseteq\mathrm{Poly}_{\mathrm{mc}}^{d}\times\mathrm{Poly}^{d}$ be an irreducible subvariety defined over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ . Assume that as $(f,g)$ varies over $X(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$ , the map $f$ is not always $z^{d}$ . Fix a positive integer $k$ and let

$$ \cal{X}=(\Delta)^{k}\times X\subseteq(\mathbb{P}^{1})^{2k}\times X, $$

where we view $\cal{X}$ as a family over the base $X$ . Then the DeMarco–Mavraki conjecture is true for $\cal{X}$ .

#### Proof.

Let’s first handle the case where $\operatorname{Prep}(f_{s})=\operatorname{Prep}(g_{s})$ for every pair $(f,g)\in X(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$ . Then there exists a constant $\lambda$ so that $f=\lambda g$ is true for all pairs $(f,g)\in X(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$ with $\lambda\in\mathrm{Aut}(\cal{J}(f_{\eta})$ , where $f_{\eta}$ denotes the generic $f$ . In particular, $\cal{X}$ itself is preperiodic for $\Phi$ and hence is $\Phi$ -special. Thus $r_{\Phi,\cal{X}}=\dim\cal{X}-\dim X=k$ .

We may now verify that

$$ \widehat{T}_{\Phi}^{\wedge k}\wedge[\cal{X}]\not=0. $$

Indeed by slicing, it suffices to prove that for $s\in X(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$ , the current $\widehat{T}_{\Phi,s}^{\wedge k}$ is non-zero on the fiber $(\Delta)^{k}$ . In this case if we identify $\Delta$ with $\mathbb{P}^{1}$ , then we are looking at the current $T=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\pi_{i}^{*}(\widehat{T}_{f_{s}}+\widehat{T}_{g_{s}})$ where $\pi_{i}:(\mathbb{P}^{1})^{k}\to\mathbb{P}^{1}$ is the $i$ th projection map and $\widehat{T}_{f_{s}},\widehat{T}_{g_{s}}$ are the $(1,1)$ -dynamical currents for the pair $(f_{s},g_{s})$ . Now expanding out $T^{\wedge k}$ gives us a sum of non-negative currents, one of which is $\wedge_{i=1}^{k}\pi_{i}^{*}\widehat{T}_{f_{s}}$ , which is clearly positive as $\pi_{i}$ ’s are from independent coordinates. Hence $\widehat{T}_{\Phi}^{\wedge k}\not=0$ , which verifies the DeMarco–Mavraki conjecture in this setting.

We now assume that there is at least one pair $(f_{s},g_{s})$ such that $\operatorname{Prep}(f_{s})\not=\operatorname{Prep}(g_{s})$ . This puts us in the setting of Theorem 7.1. Note that as $(2)\implies(1)$ is already known, if one knew that $\cal{X}$ does not contain a Zariski dense set of $\Phi$ -preperiodic point then the DeMarco–Mavraki conjecture is automatically verified in this case. In particular, for $k\geq\dim X+1$ , as Theorem 7.1 implies that $\cal{X}$ does not have a Zariski dense set of $\Phi$ -preperiodic points and thus the DeMarco–Mavraki conjecture is true for $k\geq\dim X+1$ .

Now assume that $k\leq\dim X$ . Then [32, Theorem 3.1] implies that $\cal{X}$ contains a Zariski dense set of preperiodic points. It thus suffices to show that $\widehat{T}_{\Phi}^{r_{\Phi,\cal{X}}}\wedge[\cal{X}]\not=0$ . First, we have $r_{\Phi,\cal{X}}\leq 2k$ and we only need to show that $\widehat{T}_{\Phi}^{\wedge 2k}\wedge[\cal{X}]\not=0$ . When $k=\dim X$ , this is equivalent to non-degeneracy of $\cal{X}$ . This is implied by the proof of Theorem 7.1, as we have bigness of $\sum_{i=1}^{m}p_{i}^{*}\tilde{L}$ on $\cal{X}$ where $m=\dim X$ , using again [105, Theorem 4.1], which gives us non-degeneracy of $\cal{X}$ .

For $k<\dim X$ , let us assume for contradiction that $\widehat{T}_{\Phi}^{\wedge 2k}\wedge[\cal{X}]=0$ . Identifying $\Delta$ with $\mathbb{P}^{1}$ again and letting $\pi_{i}:\Delta^{k}\times X\to\Delta\times X$ be the projection to the $i$ th coordinate, we have that

$$ \left(\sum_{i=1}^{k}(\pi_{i}^{*}\widehat{T}_{f}+\pi_{i}^{*}\widehat{T}_{g})\right)^{\wedge 2k}=0\text{ on }\Delta^{k}\times X. $$

On the other hand for $m=\dim X$ , we have

$$ \left(\sum_{i=1}^{m}(\pi_{i}^{*}\widehat{T}_{f}+\pi_{i}^{*}\widehat{T}_{g})\right)^{\wedge 2m}\not=0\text{ on }\Delta^{m}\times X. $$

We now expand out (7.2). Since $\widehat{T}_{f}^{2}=\widehat{T}_{g}^{2}=0$ (see [55]), the only surviving term is

$$ \pi_{1}^{*}\widehat{T}_{f}\wedge\pi_{1}^{*}\widehat{T}_{g}\wedge\cdots\wedge\pi_{m}^{*}\widehat{T}_{f}\wedge\pi_{m}^{*}\widehat{T}_{g}. $$

Now let $\pi:\Delta^{m}\times X\to\Delta^{k}\times X$ be the projection to the first $k$ coordinates. Then we have

$$ \pi^{*}(\pi_{1}^{*}\widehat{T}_{f}\wedge\cdots\wedge\pi_{k}^{*}\widehat{T}_{g})\wedge\pi^{*}_{k+1}\widehat{T}_{f}\wedge\cdots\wedge\pi_{m}^{*}\widehat{T}_{g}\not=0. $$

This implies that

$$ \pi_{1}^{*}\widehat{T}_{f}\wedge\cdots\wedge\pi_{k}^{*}\widehat{T}_{g}\not=0\text{ on }\Delta^{k}\times X, $$

contradicting (7.1). Hence $\widehat{T}_{\Phi}^{\wedge 2k}\wedge[\cal{X}]\not=0$ as desired. ∎
